title: Breaking: Cricket Australia agrees to bring private investment to Big Bash
text:
Cricket Australia has agreed to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

The Cricket Australia (CA) board made the announcement on Tuesday, with the sale process of the Renegades to be the first venture into bringing private investment into the franchise T20 league.

CA is hoping the Renegades will play under new ownership for the 2027/28 Big Bash season.

Depending on the success of the Renegades sale, CA said in a statement on Tuesday that it would "consider taking other clubs to market under a self-determination model that gives each State member the ability to assess the optimal pathway for its own club and community".

title: Edge Early Learning Centre closed after child hospitalised
text:
Edge Early Learning in Port Augusta has been forced to close for two weeks after an incident which resulted in the hospitalisation of a child attending the service last Thursday.

The Education Standards Board (ESB) found the provider contravened it's responsibility to protect children from harm and hazards.

The centre will be closed until Monday, September 21 at 6:30pm.

Education Minister Lucy Hood described the incident as "an allergen management issue".

"[It was] in regards to a young child being served food that they shouldn't have been served and I understand it led to the hospitalisation of a child," she said.

"My understanding was that the child had several allergies.

"Allergen management has clearly been a challenge for the Edge Early Learning centres.

"The service has been closed for 14 days. Parents have been notified, and they'll be encouraged to seek alternative options during this closure period."

The ESB also ordered the centre to provide written communication to the families of all children enrolled at the service which outlines the incident and the ESB's subsequent directions.

Edge will also need to undertake an investigation into the incident and "provide independent training to all service staff that includes emergency response".

Edge Early Learning has been contacted for comment.

Late last month, Edge — which also has centres in the ACT and Queensland, in addition to those in South Australia — entered voluntary administration.

In a statement at the time, it said administrators KordaMentha had been appointed to "review the business", and that the process would allow the company "to assess its financial position and consider options for its future".

title: Lion turns down monster offer from rival as Saint demands trade
text:
Brisbane Lions premiership hero Zac Bailey has re-signed with the reigning premiers, ending a long-running saga about whether he would move to Adelaide.

In an added subplot to this Saturday night's semifinal between the Lions and the Crows at the Gabba, Bailey has turned down a monster offer from Adelaide.

The restricted free agent has penned a new eight-year deal to remain with the Lions until the end of 2034.

A two-time All-Australian, Bailey has enjoyed another outstanding season with 31 goals and averaged a career-high 21.7 disposals.

The 26-year-old's call comes as the Lions prepare to farewell star veteran Lachie Neale, who is expected to move to Collingwood during the trade period.

Bailey's signature comes just three days after the Lions were unexpectedly smashed by Sydney in the qualifying final at the SCG.

Marshall demands trade from Saints, Duursma wants to leave Roos

Meanwhile, Rowan Marshall is demanding a trade from St Kilda, a year after Geelong tried to lure the experienced ruckman.

Rowan Marshall wants to be traded away from St Kilda. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

Marshall is contracted at the Saints until the end of next season, with the Cats and Essendon his strongest suitors.

He tried to leave for Geelong at the end of last season but has not yet nominated his preferred new club.

Cats coach Chris Scott was tight-lipped on his club's prospects of signing the 30-year-old.

"If I was [interested], I wouldn't tell you," Scott told reporters on Tuesday.

"It's an unfortunate situation. I think everyone would like us all to be a bit more open, but I think it's got to the stage now [where] the communication should be driven by the players themselves.

"I don't think it's our place to sort of speak on their behalf, so it's probably a question better directed at him."

Scott said the fact Marshall remained contracted at the Saints complicated matters.

Marshall played 21 games this season for the Saints, who opted for ex-Carlton recruit Tom de Koning as the club's first-choice ruck.

St Kilda said it would consider its options ahead of the trade period, which opens on October 5.

"Marshall has not nominated a preferred destination at this stage, with the club making clear that any trade will need to be in the best interests of the St Kilda Football Club," the statement said.

Meanwhile, the fourth pick from the 2023 draft, Zane Duursma, has told North Melbourne he wants to move to Melbourne.

Loading...

The Demons have long been linked to the 21-year-old, who has played 38 games for the Kangaroos in three seasons.

Duursma has resisted signing a fresh three-year contract offer from the Roos, who last week sacked veteran coach Alastair Clarkson.

The Demons are understood to have separately told former captain Jack Viney that he is welcome to explore a trade after an injury-cruelled season.

Viney, 32, played only one game — in Melbourne's wildcard finals loss to Carlton — after having pre-season Achilles surgery and then suffering back and toe injuries.

Viney, a premiership player in 2021, is contracted until the end of 2028.

AAP

title: Dutchman who knocked de Minaur out of US Open stages epic comeback
text:
Dutch tennis player Botic van de Zandschulp saved match point to avoid losing in straight sets, before staging a huge comeback to advance to the US Open quarterfinals.

The 30-year-old, who downed Australian Alex de Minaur in a second-round upset at Flushing Meadows, was on the brink of defeat against Frenchman Arthur Gea but recovered to make it to a grand slam quarterfinal for the second time in his career.

Gea, who got into the main draw tournament when 2022 runner-up Casper Ruud pulled out with a back injury, was trying to become the first lucky loser to make a men's singles grand slam quarterfinal.

After winning the opening two sets, Gea had match point in the third-set tiebreaker, but van de Zandschulp saved that, then staged his comeback to claim a 3-6, 6-7(0), 7-6(7), 7-6(3), 6-4 victory in 5 hours, 13 minutes.

It was the fourth-longest match in US Open history.

"I think this is probably better than the first quarterfinal I made here," van de Zandschulp said, referring to his other US Open quarterfinal appearance in 2021.

"It hasn't sunk in yet, but I think tomorrow it's going to be a great feeling."

Number 28 seed Alexander Blockx beat 24th seed Francisco Cerundolo 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5 to become the first man from Belgium to reach the US Open quarterfinals, where he will play Karen Khachanov.

Khachanov also needed five sets to advance to the quarterfinal stage, downing American 14th seed Learner Tien 7-5, 4-6, 6-7(6), 6-1, 6-4.

Men's number one seed Alexander Zverev is playing the final match of the day against Italian 21st seed Luciano Darderi.

ABC/AP

title: Border Force seizes 1.7m cigarettes, thousands of vapes in WA, NT raids
text:
The Australian Border Force (ABF) has seized more than a million illegal cigarettes and vapes in a series of raids throughout Western Australia and the Northern Territory in a joint operation with other federal, state and territory agencies.

In a statement today, an ABF spokesperson said Operation Tempest uncovered more than 1.7 million cigarettes and 504 kilograms of loose-leaf tobacco, along with more than 9,500 vapes and 6,310 oral nicotine pouches across 66 locations.

The spokesperson said the haul would have had a street value of more than $814,000 and represented almost $4 million in foregone taxes.

Law enforcement agencies raided 13 locations in Darwin and Katherine late last month, seizing more than 300kg of loose-leaf tobacco. (Supplied: ABF)

They said 66 people of interest were also identified during the six-day blitz late last month and authorities had applied for the closure of 15 shops as a result.

In the NT alone, the spokesperson said NT Health and Australian Taxation Office inspectors found more than 300,000 cigarettes, 306 kg of loose-leaf tobacco, more than 1,560 vapes and almost 3,000 oral nicotine pouches at 13 locations across Darwin and Katherine.

The sites included two car yards, a petrol station, eight shops, a postal depot and a residential property in Stuart Park, with the raids also turning up electronic devices, NSW number plates and drug paraphernalia.

The joint operation resulted in authorities applying for the closure of 15 shops in WA and the NT. (Supplied: ABF)

At the same time, WA Health officials searched 45 retail shops, while ABF officers in Perth, Mariginiup and Margaret River raided four storage facilities, two postal depots, a home and a shipping container stored on a rural property.

They seized more than 1.46 million cigarettes, 197 kg of loose-leaf tobacco and 7,900 vapes, along with 1,000 cigars, 3,360 oral nicotine pouches and 4 kg of MDMA, while agents screened passengers from 22 international flights for illicit tobacco.

It comes after the ABF allegedly discovered 433,400 cigarettes, 686 kg of loose-leaf tobacco and 50,200 single-use vapes inside a Darwin Storage unit in June.

ABF officers raided four storage facilities, two postal depots, a home and a shipping container in WA, finding more than a million cigarettes. (Supplied: ABF)

A month earlier, 103,600 illegally imported cigarettes and 39 kg of loose-leaf tobacco were also seized from an international mail carrier.

In a statement, ABF Commander Greg Dowse said criminals were working to "diversify" their activities "in an attempt to conceal their operations and maximise profits".

"No single agency can address illicit tobacco networks alone," he said.

The joint operation uncovered more than 9,500 vapes and 6,310 oral nicotine pouches across 66 locations. (Supplied: ABF)

"Success comes from coordinated action where intelligence, analytical capabilities, regulatory powers and enforcement actions are brought together to target the full criminal ecosystem, not just individual detections or actors."

Australian Federal Police Detective Acting Superintendent Pixie Fuhrmeister said the agency would continue to work with its law enforcement partners to "proactively target" and "disrupt" those involved.

The agents screened passengers from 22 international flights for illicit tobacco as part of Operation Tempest. (Supplied: ABF)

"The illicit tobacco trade is directly linked to acts of violence in our community and these crimes are executed by organised crime groups in their pursuit of power and profit," she said.

"Anyone who becomes involved in the illicit activity should be warned the AFP and its partners are committed to ongoing action to stop criminal enterprises profiting from everyday Australians."

As of today, authorities say there have been no arrests or charges laid in either jurisdiction.

title: Australia has a housing shortage but builders are still collapsing. Why?
text:
Across Australia, thousands of people are waiting to find out if their homes will be built, after several separate construction company collapses.

By far the biggest of those recent collapses has been the Bathla Group, a Sydney developer that's been one of Australia's largest affordable home builders.

Owing about $3.4 billion to private lenders, Bathla's voluntary administration has thrown the construction of more than 2,000 apartments into limbo, while jeopardising a further pipeline of 14,000 homes.

More builders going bust since COVID

Figures released last week show 3,472 Australian construction companies went bust in the financial year to June 30 2026: one in four (24.5 per cent) of all company insolvencies nationally.

The only good news? The number of builder insolvencies was slightly down for the first time since a steep rise began during COVID.

However, our research has found insolvencies in the construction sector remain consistently higher than in other industries. That makes it harder to build the housing we need.

Australia is falling further behind in meeting the federal government's 1.2 million new homes goal by 2029. Official forecasts released last month indicate the target won't be met until December 2030. New South Wales — Australia's largest housing market — may not meet its targets until March 2032, three years late on a five-year target.

There's no shortage of demand for new homes. What we lack is a construction system capable of delivering them reliably, sustainably and at scale.

Loading...

Bathla's financial ripple effects

On Monday, more than 200 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down as the administrator continues to work on a rescue deal.

While most of its building projects are in Western Sydney, Bathla's collapse is being watched around Australia because of its wider financial impacts.

Like any company collapse, there are specific circumstances involved in Bathla's current woes. Its business model relied on high volumes of low-cost building.

The NSW building regulator has also conducted more than 40 inspections of Bathla sites in recent months, and ordered the builder to fix serious defects in one major development.

Bathla may have taken as many as 1,000 deposits from buyers for homes now stalled. But home buyers aren't the only people affected.

'Troubling developments' in private credit

As well as owing money to subcontractors, Bathla owes money to a long list of non‑bank lenders — also known as private credit firms.

This reflects the construction industry's heavy reliance on alternative finance, because banks have reduced their exposure to riskier lending.

On Friday, Australian Securities and Investments Commission chair Sarah Court said the corporate watchdog was closely following "several troubling developments in the private credit sector, most notably with the recent collapse of Bathla".

Court pointed out that many Australians are exposed to private credit through their superannuation funds — meaning "this is not some peripheral issue".

Owing about $3.4 billion to private lenders, Bathla's voluntary administration has thrown the construction of more than 2,000 apartments into limbo, while jeopardising a further pipeline of 14,000 homes. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The perfect storm hitting builders

Bathla is not an isolated case. The wider construction industry is under strain, with higher costs, thinner profit margins and rising risks.

Figures released last month show house construction costs are now 51 per cent higher than before COVID.

For builders with slim profit margins, the rise in costs can make some projects uneconomic.

With costs rising unpredictably, builders locked into fixed-price contracts are absorbing losses they cannot sustain. This was a major driver of the spike in builder insolvencies during COVID.

Falling house prices and poor market sentiment mean some projects no longer stack up financially.

Many investors and buyers are spooked by three interest rate rises this year, higher costs, and recent federal budget changes to housing tax concessions that have made housing less attractive to investors. The prospect of further interest rate increases is also likely to see projects stalled, as the market waits for conditions to improve.

Then there are ongoing shortages of tradespeople. On top of those, home builders are now competing with data centre builders for tradies, which has driven up salaries.

Little wonder construction insolvencies have risen back to pre-COVID levels, despite strong demand for housing.

Structural change is needed

Governments can't fix all the problems we face, such as price hikes driven by the Middle East war.

Bathla suspensions point to 'larger storm' Under voluntary administration and having stood down two-thirds its staff, embattled property developer Bathla Group leaves dozens of projects in limbo.

But federal, state and local governments are increasingly recognising their role in creating structural barriers to building more homes.

A Productivity Commission draft report released in July identified many of the problems we need to address, including restrictive land-use regulation, slow and inconsistent approvals, poor coordination on key infrastructure, and complex regulation. These all increase costs and delays.

Our 2025 report showed over-regulation is particularly hard on small builders, who struggle to comply with overlapping national, state and local requirements. That matters because our research also showed almost two-thirds (63 per cent) of building company collapses were concentrated among small builders.

The National Construction Code is another challenge. Even with some states deferring 2025 code changes, the national rules remain complex and frequently updated — again, making compliance difficult for small builders.

What's safer than houses?

Some builders are responding by pivoting to infrastructure and commercial projects, such as Victoria's Big Housing Build or Queensland's Olympics construction projects. These can offer more manageable terms and less exposure to market volatility.

Good builders can pick and choose their work. Right now, housing is the riskiest option on the table.

Until that changes, we're likely to see more Australian builders moving away from creating the homes we urgently need — along with more headlines about another builder going bust.

Lyndall Bryant is a senior lecturer and Amanda Bull is a lecturer at the Queensland University of Technology. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

title: My 'friendship cupid' gave me connections I didn't think were possible
text:
I call my friend Isabel "friendship cupid".

To be clear, Isabel is not a cherub, and she doesn't carry a bow and arrow.

But she is a matchmaker of a different kind: the reason I have made several new and cherished friends.

It's been hard for me to make friends as an adult. My ever-present anxiety tells me it would be far safer to stay silent and isolated than to reach out and risk rejection.

I'm a wheelchair user and one of the few people still taking precautions against COVID, due to the impact these symptoms could have on my health. This means there are limited public spaces I can access safely and limited opportunities to meet new people in person.

That's why Isabel is so important to me.

She not only sees the opportunity for connection, but takes action to foster that connection.

When I don't believe in myself enough to reach out, she can be a friendship cupid for me.

Here's how it happened

Not long after Isabel and I became housemates, she encouraged me to message her sister, Matilda, because we have a lot in common.

Laura says encouragement has helped her forge lasting friendships. (Supplied: Laura Pettenuzzo)

I took a few months to reach out, because even with Isabel's prompting, I was anxious, perhaps even more than I would have been without it.

What if Matilda and I didn't get along? What would I tell Isabel? Would I have failed some implicit test if Matilda didn't like me?

I didn't need to worry. Matilda and I clicked instantly, our conversation flowing naturally.

With Matilda, three hours often feels like five minutes, and there's still so much more we could say to one another.

We live several hours apart and don't see each other in person often, but I'm always enlivened when we do.

Isabel's matchmaking was spot on, and she is far from the only friendship cupid I've been lucky enough to encounter.

One of my former co-workers told me repeatedly how similar I was to her friend Nic, how our lives had so many parallels. When she started a group chat with the three of us, and invited Nic and I to a group video call, I saw immediately that she was right.

Laura (second from left) with three friends, including Shirley (left) and Kate (second from right). (Supplied: Laura Petenuzzo)

Nic and I have been friends for almost five years now and in that time she's supported stuck by me through good times and bad. She's celebrated my achievements and stuck by me as I've made many mistakes.

When I've struggled with my mental health, I've hurt her and pushed her away. But she's been gracious enough to listen to me apologise and take accountability. She has forgiven me.

I'm attending her wedding at the end of this year, all thanks to that one video chat.

Nic and I are also a great example of the success of friendship cupids creating friendship groups.

As well as introducing me to her sister, Isabel also introduced me to her best friend, Nicola. Matilda, Nicola and I have a group chat, and I have a photo of the three of us stuck to my fridge. Fittingly, I met Isabel through another friend, our bond another match well made.

I hope that one day, I can continue the friendship chain, can pay it forward and be a friendship cupid for someone else.

The lasting impact

While this whole process sounds a little like networking, I prefer to think of it as something much more than that.

My friendship cupid cared enough to build connections between others, without expecting anything in return. Without expecting these connections to last the distance.

Even though rejection from a potential friend might hurt, it doesn't mean I stop trying (I might just hibernate for a few days to pull myself back together).

The beauty I've discovered is in my willingness to be open to connection, and to facilitate that connection for other people.

Not everyone has that willingness, but I've found that some people — my people — do, and our lives are better for it.

title: Live: Waitlists, distance, or no bulk billing: Have your say on healthcare barriers
text:
Seeing a specialist in a regional area is next to impossible. The waiting times are months or even years and the consults are then so short (due to the specialist’s limited time and often overbooking) problems aren’t even addressed. What is or could be done to address this issue.

Our guest expert Peter has answered your question below, Michael.

You're spot on, and the data backs you up.

People in rural areas get much less specialist care, and the places with the least care of all are almost all in rural areas. Half of remote and very remote areas receive less than one specialist service per person a year. There's nowhere in a major city with that little care.

There are a couple of good ways to fix this.

One is to train more specialists in rural areas, which makes them more likely to stay there when they finish their training. Governments should set targets for rural training, and tie funding for training places to meeting those targets.

Another solution is building up public clinics in the areas with the least care. Today, the areas with the least private care don't get more public care. That's one big reason for the long waits in many rural areas. Governments should set a minimum level of care that every community can expect. Then areas with the least care should be the first to get more public appointments.

New public clinics in rural areas might have to run a bit differently, for example using more telehealth. But the key is committing to a minimum level of care, investing in more public appointments, and making sure they go to the communities that need them most.

title: Car plunges into suburban sinkhole in Perth's south
text:
A burst water main in Perth's south has caused a car to plunge into a sinkhole overnight, cutting off the water supply to nearby homes.

The sedan has fallen into a large hole in the middle of The Bridgeway, one of the key suburban roads running through Canning Vale.

The car became stuck around 4am on Tuesday after the road gave way. (ABC News)

In a statement, the Water Corporation confirmed the car became stuck around 4am after driving through floodwater following a burst water main.

"Crews were onsite within 30 minutes and promptly isolated the main, with work now underway to remove the vehicle and make repairs," the Water Corporation said.

"Water supply is affected to around 10 nearby homes, and residents may notice discoloured water as repairs progress."

Workers at the scene in Canning Vale, a suburb about 22 kilometres from Perth's CBD. (ABC News)

The Water Corporation's website showed the outages as at 11.30am were still affecting several streets in Canning Vale and Thornlie, including The Bridgeway, Gateway Boulevard and Figtree Drive.

'Extremely rare'

The Water Corporation's Paul Prottey said while burst pipes were not uncommon, it was rare for one to cause a sinkhole.

"With a network the size that we have across Perth, we get our leaks and bursts, like every other water scheme across the world," he told 102.5 ABC Perth.

"But to have a car fall into a hole in the middle of a road is an extremely rare occurrence."

The back wheels of the car were left perched right on the edge of the sinkhole. (ABC News)

Mr Prottey said it would be difficult to remove the car given how close the water pipe was to the gas main.

"We've got a tow truck on site, we just don't want to remove that car until we get the [water main] isolated … we'll just do it as carefully and safely as we can," he said.

Mr Prottey said it was too early to say whether the incident would cause broader issues with the water network.

It is rare for burst water pipes to cause sinkholes. (ABC News)

"We'll check the failure of the pipe once we get [the car] out and see what the cause is, so we can ascertain if that's going to happen anywhere else and see what we can do to prevent it in the future," he said.

'That could've been anybody'

Local resident Fred Sin said it was "crazy" to see a gaping hole open up on a street he used every day to do the school run.

"Imagine if I am the one driving on the road and if this happened, it's shocking, I have three grandkids in my car," he said.

Fred Sin says he was "shocked" to see a sinkhole open up on the road he uses during the school run. (ABC News)

Another resident, Richard Junior, said he was surprised when his wife received a text from a friend mentioning the sinkhole on a road he used all the time.

"To see something like that, that could've been anybody," he said.

He said in his 20 years of living in the suburb, he had never seen as much disruption.

"I've heard of sinkholes and black holes, but you know, we live in Canning Vale. It's a first for me," he said.

Carol and Barry Stalker said they were awoken by a loud bang in the early hours of the morning but did not realise what had happened until the next morning.

The area in front of Carol and Barry Stalker's house was temporarily flooded. (ABC News)

"We walked out and it was unbelievable to see the car in the hole, it was a mess," Mr Stalker said.

He said their water had been disconnected for about an hour.

No injuries were reported to St John WA and no ambulance was sent to the incident.

Traffic management is in place and drivers have been asked to avoid the area while repairs are undertaken.

title: Under pressure to explain super policy, Joyce says he is 'not Jesus Christ'
text:
One Nation Treasury spokesperson Barnaby Joyce has struggled to explain the impact of the party's proposed early superannuation access scheme, saying he is "not Jesus Christ" while being questioned about the policy's financial and economic consequences.

Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or have a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.

The money would retain the favourable tax concession Australians already receive on super savings under the plan, which One Nation said would provide "breathing room" for people struggling with the cost of living.

Are the super wars another Mediscare? A political war over superannuation has been inflamed in the past fortnight.

On Tuesday, Mr Joyce sidestepped questions about modelling of the proposal after economists warned it could have an inflationary impact.

"The implications that I have to model you getting your own money, I find a little bit perverse. It is actually your money," he said.

He later said one reason One Nation had not modelled their policy was because Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had not awarded the minor party additional staff and resourcing.

When pushed on the loss of people's retirement savings over time, Mr Joyce insisted he was across the detail of the policy.

"I'm the Treasury spokesman, not Jesus Christ. I mean, you have to actually give me the details of these things, if you got to put them forward to me," he told 7.30 on Monday.

Australians 'not stupid', Joyce says

Mr Joyce argued the money in retirement savings was already circulating in the economy because it was being invested via superannuation companies, and therefore would not be inflationary.

Independent economist Saul Eslake said he found the comments "disturbing" because they showed a lack of understanding from Mr Joyce about how the economy works.

Can you access your super savings before retirement? Should you tap into your super early? There is a trade-off between instant cash and future growth.

Mr Eslake said money that is invested in superannuation is used to buy shares, government bonds and investments in overseas markets, which means it is not circulating in the Australian economy and adding to demand for goods and services.

"If you instead take money out of superannuation so that there is less invested in financial and real investment assets, and instead it is sitting at least initially in a bank account, which history shows [people] are likely to withdraw to fund to use on additional spending, it will then go into the economy," he said.

He warned pumping more cash into the economy would put upward pressure on inflation, and said the Reserve Bank would likely be forced to increase interest rates.

Mr Joyce also said "anyone with a brain" would be able to effectively use the scheme, which would not be means tested.

"People are not stupid," he said.

"The presumption by the socialists is that everyone's a total moron and is going to take money from a good return and take it to a bad return if they don't need it.

"If there's extra money in the economy and you put it into your bank account and don't spend it, it has no inflationary aspect."

But Mr Eslake said people, especially those on lower incomes, historically did not save additional salary, but spent it.

"What evidence shows us from a wide range of studies over a long period of time is that people on lower incomes, and younger people, are more likely to spend any additional income they get compared to higher income people," he said.

"It's human nature, unfortunately, that most of us, whether we think we are smart or have had less education than others, find it difficult to make short-term sacrifices for long-term gain."

ABC accused of 'socialist' agenda

One Nation announced its policy on Monday, and Mr Joyce has since accused the ABC of being "socialists", pointing to a line of questioning in a number of interviews about the modelling of the proposal.

"I understand the ABC socialist position, that it's not really your money, it's somebody else's money. Therefore, you have to go through a bureaucracy before you get entitled to get your own money," he told ABC Radio Breakfast.

He said it was a "philosophical view" that distorted the reality of the inflationary impacts of the proposal.

"This money is your money," he said.

title: 'Buffel bust' sees volunteers clear more than 100sq/m in Alice Springs
text:
For Western Arrernte artist Carita Coultard, painting bush tucker that has been found across the nation's central desert for millennia is a chance to celebrate the region's bounty, but it also comes with an alarming message.

Her watercolour work depicts different foods she remembers collecting as a child in Hermannsburg, about 130 kilometres west of Alice Springs, which she laments "we don't see around anymore".

As the artist describes each plant, offering their names in English and her first language — including "the bush onion (yalka), the bush potato (lutjia) and all these sultanas (kutjirra ntjirrka)" — she points the finger at the invasive weed, buffel grass, for wiping them from the landscape.

Carita Coultard says buffel grass has wiped out many of the plants that feature in her paintings. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"I think about in childhood we used to just go around, walk around and get all these bush foods, but we can't see it now," Coultard said.

"We don't see them anymore around, especially around in the Alice area; like maybe way, way from town area, way up bush you might find some.

"It's so sad we can't even see.

" It's just no good at all — buffel grass is everywhere growing. "

A wet winter in the Alice Springs region has created prime conditions for buffel grass to flourish.

The hardy, drought-resistant grass was declared a weed in the Northern Territory in 2024 and spreads easily, smothering native plants and fuelling fire.

Introduced to control erosion and feed cattle in the 1960s, buffel grass spread from Central Australia and is now found in all states and territories except Tasmania and the ACT.

Carita Coultard's paintings are on display at the Olive Pink Botanic Gardens from today. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

To highlight concern over the invasive weed, Coultard and a group of artists have created an exhibition that opened at the Olive Pink Botanic Gardens in Alice Springs today.

The works have been painted on buffel paper handmade in the Many Hands art centre studio.

"You can just cut it all down in pieces … just boil it all in a pot … we just leave it to soak down, get real fluffy … blend it and then put on the mesh and put it outside to let it dry," Coultard said.

The artworks are painted on material hand made from buffel grass. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"The first lot was so rough. It was testing, trying to bring it smooth.

"We don't have a proper machine. We can just do what we can do here."

Buffel busting ahead of fire season

In another part of Alice Springs, a group of volunteers are battling buffel along the Todd River.

Its rampant run has sparked concerns of a big fire season, where excess fuel loads and predictions of a hot El Nino summer have residents on high alert.

Landcare volunteer Steve Eldgridge says he has seen change over the past 20 years where "buffel grass has really started to take over and what we see now is almost a monoculture".

Ben McIntyre and Steve Eldgridge have joined a weekly "buffel bust" to clear an area of more than 100 square metres near the centre of town. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"Our aim is really to protect these huge … lovely big old red gums that grow along the Todd River," he said.

"Obviously with so much grass growth underneath, they're at real risk of fire and we just want to stop that happening.

" I've seen so many of these 300, 400-year-old trees burn down and we're left with very few of them now. "

Since May, a weekly "buffel bust" has seen volunteers clock around 150 hours to clear an area of about 5 hectares near the centre of town.

Charles Darwin University professor Kamaljit Sangha co-authored an economic impact assessment commissioned by the NT government that looked at the cost and benefits of the spread of buffel using a model of the grass established in 1,000 hectares.

"We looked more from societal perspective thinking whole of the society, including the pastoral sector, the conservation, tourism, public and the Indigenous sectors," she said.

Declared a weed in the NT in 2024, the hardy, drought-resistant buffel grass spreads easily, smothers native plants and fuels fire. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"We know that buffel grass has spread into other landscapes where it's not wanted, so the costs are about 60 times higher than the benefits that accrue to the pastoral sector."

She said the results were conservative and a key recommendation included a coordinated approach to managing the weed.

"The costs are going to be huge because there is no natural barrier for buffel not to spread to other places," she said.

"It's not just the cost with the spread of buffel for biodiversity, the most important thing is the public costs for managing fire in the landscape."

Not yet a weed of national significance

In response, NT Lands, Planning and Environment Minister Joshua Burgoyne has written to the federal government seeking funding to support buffel management.

But the federal government is in the final stages of assessing if buffel will be declared a weed of national significance.

In late July, the National Biosecurity Committee found the invasive grass met the criteria but cited "a need to undertake further work".

The federal government is considering declaring buffel a weed of national significance. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

A statement through Weeds Australia said consensus was not reached as: "Buffel grass presents a unique and complex case that requires further consideration. It is a highly valued pasture for the cattle industry. Conversely, buffel grass has significant negative impacts."

A committee working group has been holding stakeholder meetings in every affected state, but a meeting hasn't been scheduled in the NT.

The Department of Agriculture said the committee will refer to the Territory government's buffel grass strategy and plan as it makes a final decision, which is expected by the end of the year.

title: Erin Phillips and Bruce McAvaney given SANFL's highest honour
text:
South Australia's Football Hall of Fame has inducted its first woman, former Port Adelaide and Adelaide Crows player Erin Phillips, at the SANFL's Magarey Medal count on Monday.

Phillips was one of four inductees recognised. Long-serving AFL commentator Bruce McAvaney, former Norwood player Neil Button and former Sturt player Tony Burgan were also granted South Australian Football's highest recognition.

Phillips was raised in Adelaide, where her father Greg was a multiple premiership player for Port Adelaide in the SANFL. She played junior football until her teenage years, but switched to basketball due to limited female football opportunities.

She played for the Adelaide Lightning in the WNBL and later made her mark on the world stage as a double WNBA championship player.

Bruce McAvaney called more than 1,000 AFL games. (Supplied: Channel Seven)

Returning to Australia, she joined the Adelaide Crows as captain for the first AFL Women's season in 2017. She played in three AFLW premierships, twice won the AFLW's best and fairest award and was named best-on-ground in the 2017 and 2019 AFLW Grand Finals.

She later joined Port Adelaide for the 2022 AFLW season as its inaugural captain.

"All I wanted to do was to play footy and be like Dad," Phillips said.

"I could've missed that opportunity, and I get so many women that come up to me that played or just wish they had the opportunity [and] that missed the boat.

" So, every game I felt that I was never going to take it for granted. "

McAvaney began calling SANFL matches in 1978 and went on to call more than 1,000 VFL/AFL games and 20 grand finals during his career.

"I felt like I'd reached Mount Everest by calling a South Australian league grand final in 1983," McAvaney said. "I had no idea what would happen afterwards."

The Norwood Football Club's Nik Rokahr won the Magarey Medal for the SANFL's best and fairest player on Monday night, after recording one of the highest vote tallies in the medal's history.

He was named best afield in 10 of Norwood's 18 games.

Nik Rokahr of Norwood Football Club won the 2026 Magarey Medal. (Supplied: Channel Seven)

His success makes him the first player to have won both a Magarey Medal and a WAFL Sandover Medal.

"[It's] a little bit harder to compare my year in the WAFL, but I feel it was my strongest season," Rokahr said.

Norwood last week won through to the SANFL Grand Final, when it will compete for its 32nd title against the winner of Sunday's preliminary final between Sturt and Woodville-West Torrens.

title: The grassroots queer clubs popping up in regional Queensland
text:
With no permanent LGBTQIA+ venue on the Sunshine Coast, queer residents are creating their own safe spaces.

For Alison Nolan, the lack of options meant travelling outside the region.

"Every queer person I've spoken to on the Sunshine Coast has the same comment," Ms Nolan said.

"There's nowhere to go, no events, no spaces specific to queer people."

Inspired by a club in Brisbane, Ms Nolan and co-founder Lucy Upston established a social club that runs events including trivia, picnics and games nights for queer women and gender-diverse people.

Attendance is increasing at the Lesbian Social Club. (Supplied: Alison Nolan)

Ms Nolan said the need was clear.

"Having a place where you can show up and be your true authentic self without hesitation and without having to explain is something that is so important," she said.

Grace Manning started an LGBTQIA+ run club after moving to the region about a year ago.

"I was really missing that queer community," Ms Manning said, adding that finding queer belonging locally had been "really special".

The LGBT Run Club engages in a range of active activities and "treats" afterwards. (Supplied: Grace Manning)

"If you don't see a particular box [you fit into] or you don't see yourself in your peers, you just feel lonely and isolated."

Community adapting

Queensland Council for LGBTI Health chief executive Rebecca Reynolds said queer spaces traditionally centred on bars and clubs, but that was changing with the growth of social and wellness-focused groups.

" Maybe what we're seeing isn't the disappearance of queer community spaces so much as a broadening of our imagination about what queer community space can be. "

Rebecca Reynolds says geographic isolation is one of many intersecting barriers that may impact LGBTQIA+ communities in regional towns. (Supplied: Rebecca Reynolds)

She said what was happening on the Sunshine Coast was "unique" and an example of the community "responding to its own needs".

"The more places of safety and belonging we can grow, the better off we will all be," she said.

Maroochydore had a dedicated queer cafe in recent years, but it closed its doors after less than two years due to "mounting financial challenges".

Aqualicious, a Queensland Masters swimming club for LGBTQIA+ people, expanded to the Sunshine Coast two years ago.

Aqualicious has been operating in Brisbane since 2003, but only started on the Sunshine Coast two years ago. (Supplied: Isaac Goessling)

President Isaac Goessling said the club deliberately avoided being "overly rainbow", catering to people at different stages of their queer journeys as well as allies.

"A lot of our members have perhaps only just come out about their sexuality and who they are," he said.

"Whereas some of our members go to every single Pride event."

Mr Goessling said sporting environments could be "jarring" and "not particularly safe" for queer people.

Homophobia in sports

In 2024, the Free to Exist report found LGBTQIA+ young people were 50 per cent less likely to participate in a sporting club than the broader community.

"For us … it's not even a question; it's just, 'Come and swim,'" Mr Goessling said.

" It doesn't matter who you are, but you're safe here and we value you for who you are. "

Aqualicious welcomes a range of people from 25 to 65, from working professionals to travellers, and LGBTQIA+ members to allies. (Supplied: Isaac Goessling)

Mr Goessling said the club was about more than swimming.

"It's about engaging in healthy lifestyles, getting coffee together, doing bits and pieces of our life together and just being who we are," he said.

Connection overcomes isolation

James Fowler, an affiliate research fellow at the University of Queensland's Schools of Psychology, said social connection was one of the "biggest predictors of mortality".

James Fowler's work involves research to address the mental health needs of communities, with a specialist focus on LGBTQIA+ issues. (Supplied: James Fowler)

"As you get older, a lack of social connection can have really devastating health impacts," Dr Fowler said, adding that fear could be a powerful driver of isolation, and connection could help to overcome it.

"Opportunities to connect are so important for people to see other people like them, to have role models who have faced similar things to them that maybe they won't get from traditional media outlets or family members."

Dr Fowler said the trend on the Sunshine Coast could point to an unmet need.

" There is queer joy happening in the Sunshine Coast and people are coming together to have that shared joy, potentially coming together because there aren't any other spaces where they feel safe to do so. "

A Sunshine Coast Council representative said it was "committed to fostering a community where everyone feels welcome, respected and connected, regardless of their background, identity or circumstance".

The representative said community facilities were designed to be inclusive for all members of the community, and that it had provided grant funding to LGBTQIA+ events such as the Pride Festival Fair Day and the Rangebow Festival.

Ms Nolan said she hoped to see places of safety for queer people continue to grow on the coast.

"You can't really put into words how important having a space where you can just be your true authentic self is," she said.

title: Growers forced to find off-farm incomes after fruit fly financial hit
text:
On a building site hundreds of kilometres away from his home, Jody Miltenoff works to make an income to offset the financial losses of Queensland fruit fly.

He has taken on a contract as project manager on a new hotel development in Port Adelaide, leaving his son to run his nursery business in Cambrai and orchards in Sunlands.

Mr Miltenoff said managing his jujube business from afar was challenging.

Jody Miltenoff says while he enjoys project management, he prefers farm life. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

But between extreme heatwaves last summer damaging most of his crop and the ongoing cost of fruit fly management, he was glad to have a safety net.

"I'm lucky that I've got the construction industry to fall back on and supplement our income," Mr Miltenoff said.

" I've heard of some apricot growers that are getting close to retirement and just walking away, just saying that it's too hard. "

Mr Miltenoff said sending some of his dried jujubes to Tokyo had been a boon but the loss of his fresh fruit market access had been tough.

Jujubes are a small, sweet fruit sometimes called a Chinese date or red date. (ABC Landline: Kerry Staight)

Sending fruit to his main market of Adelaide requires costly cold treatment or fumigation, while shipping to the east coast means poor returns.

"Growers in the Riverland that have been affected by fruit fly have been sending to the eastern states, so they flood that market and … the prices dropped quite severely," he said.

Funding unused

The Riverland is one of two internationally recognised Pest Free Areas (PFA) in Australia, which provides growers with a trade advantage when exporting produce.

But since a Queensland fruit fly outbreak was declared in Renmark West in late December 2020, the region has been subject to rules which restrict produce movement and require approved treatments before it can be sold.

Queensland fruit fly is endemic to Australia. (Supplied: PIRSA)

State department of primary industries (PIRSA) budget data shows of the $43 million allocated for fruit fly management in the last financial year, $10 million was unspent due to fewer detections of the pest.

According to a department spokesperson, in 2024-25 there were 7,794 Queensland fruit fly detections in South Australia, while there were 4,030 detections in 2025-26.

With fruit fly deductions almost halved, Citrus SA chair Mark Doecke said it was a step in the right direction.

"Any money saving is good money saving, that's for sure," he said.

But Mr Miltenoff said it would have been worthwhile to use the funds to adopt new technology to boost eradication efforts.

A PIRSA spokesperson said in a statement that allocation of funds was subject to approval through normal state budget processes.

Pathway to pest-free

Grower industry bodies Citrus SA and Summerfruit SA organised meetings in Renmark and Waikerie last week for growers and packers to hear about a pathway to release towns in Riverland west from the fruit fly exclusion zone.

Some growers want to see more advanced fruit fly traps. (ABC Riverland: Anita Ward)

The area known as Zone Two includes the towns of Waikerie, Cadell, Holder, Sunlands and Taylorville, which have all had consistently low detections of the pest in the past 12 months.

It follows the release of Swan Reach, known as Zone One, which was officially declared fruit fly free by PIRSA last November.

Mr Doecke said PIRSA had "taken too long" to lift restrictions.

"We started talking about getting some of these areas out three years ago," he said.

Mark Doecke says fruit fly restrictions are costing the citrus industry about $20 million a year. (ABC News: Jackson Byrne)

" If we can get some of these areas out that will instil confidence back in the public and we can ask them to get behind us and keep that fight going. "

But the process to reinstate Pest Free Area status is complicated, and dependent on variables, such as the time of year because of the fruit fly life cycle.

A PIRSA spokesperson said it required "no further fruit fly detections for an agreed period of time and all protocol requirements are met".

The new homes would be built over the next 20 years over 168 hectares of eastern suburbs land, with 40 per cent of new homes to be delivered within 200 metres of a train station, with the new Woollahra heavy rail station to open in 2029. The aim of the rezoning proposal is to enable private developers to build taller and more dense projects, and there won’t be any compulsory acquisition of land.

Spider-Man has overcome the Green Goblin, Doc Ock and Venom, but his latest triumph over Titanic could be his most memorable yet. Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which landed in theatres on July 31, has now sunk James Cameron’s beloved classic, shifting the 1997 film from the top five highest-grossing movies at the global box office. Titanic enjoyed a spot in the top five for nearly three decades, even topping the list for 12 years before being dethroned in 2010. Since then, Titanic has plunged further down the rankings, even with re-releases. Now, thanks to Spidey, it’s out of the top five entirely. Spider-Man: Brand New Day swung into the top five highest-grossing movies of all time, sinking Titanic along the way. Sony/AP Granted, this doesn’t take inflation into account. Most top five lists consider the actual money accumulated at the time each movie was released (as well as revenue from any re-releases). Movie tickets were far cheaper when Titanic hit screens, so more contemporary blockbusters are bound to earn more. On an inflation-adjusted list, classics such as Gone with the Wind, Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope and The Sound of Music would quickly climb the ranks. Regardless, with Titanic now off the top handful, which films remain? Here’s a rundown of the five films that have made the most money around the world.

Advertisement

5. Ne Zha 2 This Chinese fantasy animation is the highest-grossing non-English language film in history. It proved incredibly popular in China, becoming the first film ever to take more than $US1 billion ($1.38 billion) in a single territory. However, its popularity expanded far beyond China. In Australia, it made its debut as the third-highest ranking feature at the local box office. By its second weekend, it had made $5.22 million. Though much of Ne Zha 2’s success can be attributed to love for the original film, as well as its emotional depth in storytelling and stunning visual effects, there were also reports of the film being boosted by Chinese patriotism and a social media campaign. Fans encouraged others online to watch the film in cinemas multiple times. Chinese companies also got on board, including snacks manufacturer Weilong Food, which paused operations to take 900 of its employees to see the movie.

Advertisement

4. Avatar: The Way of Water Cameron blew audiences out of the water with Avatar in 2009, but his sequel to the sci-fi epic threw them right back into it. Avatar: The Way of Water once again lured people back to the cinema to see the awe-inspiring visuals on the biggest screen possible (and, of course, in 3D). Cameron even developed entirely new technology to record actors performing in live action underwater. The long-awaited sequel brought back fan favourites such as Zoe Saldaña and Sigourney Weaver, but it also introduced new major names such as Kate Winslet. Everything these actors’ characters did on screen, the actors actually performed in real life, with the crew logging about 200,000 hours of free-diving. Winslet even smashed Tom Cruise’s previous record for longest-held breath, and held hers for a staggering seven minutes and 14 seconds (Cruise held his breath for just over six minutes in Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation). This brought an incredible air of authenticity and craft to the film, which evidently generated significant word-of-mouth. 3. Spider-Man: Brand New Day

Tom Holland’s successful run as Peter Parker continued with Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which has just enjoyed its sixth consecutive weekend atop the global box office. The film, directed by Dustin Daniel Cretton, hearkened back to Spider-Man’s roots, dropping Parker into the streets of New York where small-time criminals run amok. This return clearly paid off – the movie is currently experiencing the longest stint at No.1 since Avatar: The Way of Water in 2022. And according to Variety, Cretton’s movie is also primed to overtake Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) as the highest-grossing movie of all time at the US box office. These figures helped the Marvel film to not only bump Titanic – a cinematic behemoth that had been in the top five for nearly as long as Holland has been alive – but it also completely re-shuffled the list by overtaking both Ne Zha 2 and the Avatar sequel. 2. title: Fighting the bully: Canada throws a punch back at Trump
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyTrade wars Opinion Fighting the bully: Canada throws a punch back at Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 8, 2026 — 11:59am

September 8, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Canada’s Mark Carney has risked an escalation in trade hostilities with the US by following through with his foreshadowed retaliatory tariffs on US imports. Just after midnight on Monday, Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on about $US20 billion ($28 billion) of US exports went live, making Canada, with China, the only significant economies willing to stand up to Donald Trump’s trade bullying. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office last year. AP Photo/Evan Vucci The tariffs are a response to a similar dollar amount of new tariffs on Canada’s exports to the US that the Trump administration imposed last month after talks between the countries – held against the backdrop of Trump’s threat of those tariffs unless Canada made a range of trade concessions – broke down. While willing to accept some duties and to tighten rules of origin that might have shifted more of the North American auto industry supply chain across the border into the US, last-minute demands from the US negotiators – abolishing Canadian French language local content rules and quotas, exclusive access to Canada’s minerals and restrictions on its ability to sign trade deals with other countries – caused Carney to end the negotiations.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump would plunge the US into crisis if he carried out his latest bizarre threat Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The US proceeded with its new tariffs on Canadian autos, dairy, alcohol, metals and consumer goods and now Canada has matched them on a dollar-for-dollar basis, targeting US apparel, timber, steel and aluminium, agricultural equipment, appliances, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics. Both countries had pre-existing tariffs, dating back to Trump’s initial declaration of a trade war on the rest of the world last year, his singling out (absurdly) Canada for its alleged role in fentanyl exports to the US and, more recently, a 10 per cent rate (along with much of the rest of the world) for its claimed failure to do enough to halt imports of goods made with forced labour. Canada had responded to the earliest of those tariffs with duties of its own, but the effective rate on US imports was only just above one per cent. With this week’s counter tariffs, it is now closer to 4 per cent. The effective rate of the tariffs on Canadian imports to the US was around 3 per cent before the recent changes. It’s now closer to 6 per cent. Carney’s willingness to stand up to the US is brave, bordering on foolhardy, given that nearly 70 per cent of Canada’s exports go to the US and that he doesn’t have the rare earths monopoly that China used to force Trump to back away from his direst trade threats to its economy.

Advertisement

There is some shelter from the United States-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement (USMCA), although that hasn’t stopped Trump from targeting Canada (or Mexico) with tariffs so far. Trump has been trying to use the threat of walking away from the USMCA (which he negotiated in his first term) as leverage to force more trade concessions from Canada and Mexico (although America’s withdrawal from the USMCA would take a decade), with Mexico more willing than Canada to do a new deal. Canada is standing up for itself, but almost 70 per cent of the country’s exports go to the US. Getty Images While Canada’s retaliation might provoke even stronger action from the US – Trump has threatened more tariffs and even (along with some other major US trading partners) the end of all trade – the three economies within the USMCA are highly integrated. Canada might be harmed more, but the US would also suffer self-harm if it responds to Canada’s new tariffs by raising its own.

Advertisement

By far the largest of Canada’s exports to the US are oil and refined products. It accounts for about 60 per cent of America’s oil imports. Because the oil is extracted from oil sands and is heavy, viscous and contains sulfur and metals, it requires specialised refining. Refineries in Texas and Louisiana process the imported oil. Related Article Analysis

US politics Trump’s weekend of trolling can’t paper over his political problems Trump hasn’t included Canadian oil, yet, in his list of sanctioned products. That would be self-destructive. Canada is, however, trying to diversify the customer base for its oil (and protect itself from the threat that America might displace its exports with similarly heavy Venezuelan crude) by planning to build a pipeline from its oil fields to the Pacific coast that would give it access to the Asian market. The Canadian and US auto and auto parts industries are closely entwined – auto parts can cross the border several times (and be charged duties each time) before vehicles are fully built – so tariff disruption will hurt both economies and their US company-dominated auto industries.

Advertisement

Last year Canada exported $US9.9 billion of aluminium and aluminium products to the US, for use in the auto industry, in cans, construction and a raft of other purposes. The US gets about 70 per cent of its imported primary aluminium from Canada and nearly 60 per cent of all its aluminium and aluminium products imports. The US aluminium industry has shrunk over decades, with some of the major US producers, like Alcoa, shifting their operations to Canada, with his vast hydroelectric power resources that provide cheap electricity to an exceptionally energy-intensive sector. Canada might be harmed more, but the US would also suffer self-harm if it responds to Canada’s new tariffs by raising its own. Trump might want to use tariffs to force companies to reshore activities to the US, but the US grid doesn’t produce electricity cheaply or reliably enough (and Trump is trying to stifle renewable sources) to compete with Canada. If Trump does escalate, Canada does have options that would hurt the US, create supply shortages and raise costs for US businesses and prices for US consumers.

Advertisement

While Canada and Canadians would also suffer – unlike Trump, some in his administration and many of his MAGA supporters, they understand how tariffs work and who pays the duties – they appear prepared to accept that as the price of sovereignty. Trump’s continued rumblings about the “51st state” have drawn Canadians together in their support for Carney and his response. Carney has also been busy since winning his office in March last year, negotiating a raft of trade agreements with other countries to try to diversify his economy away from its over-reliance on the US. That, no doubt, is why Trump’s negotiators tried to restrict its ability to do trade deals with third parties. Loading Thus, in the longer term, Trump’s ill-conceived trade assault on America’s closest ally and trading partner is likely – as is the case with other allies of long-standing – to lead to a fundamental change and distancing in the economic and political relationships between the countries.

Advertisement

Trump isn’t helping to lower the temperature with his continuing threats and juvenile social media posts, including one very recently which depicts Trump skating on ice, dressed in full ice hockey gear, savagely beating Carney with a hockey stick. Related Article Trump diplomacy Hegseth enrages Canada by mocking appearance of female military cadets Trump, of course, has never been seen on skates of any kind, while Carney was a very active and competitive ice hockey player in his youth, including a stint as the reserve goalkeeper for Harvard’s team. Trump’s post is rightly being criticised, and ridiculed. Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America, continuing to post maps of the United States that include Canada as a state and referring to Carney as “governor”, aren’t going to shift the increasingly anti-American sentiment in Canada. Nor will they endear Trump to the rest of the nations that have been hit by Trump’s tariffs and will watch how Canada’s stand against Trump’s tariffs and intimidation plays out. If others showed similar resolve, Trump’s leverage – the threat of more tariffs – would be undermined. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. title: The unusual tactics some shoppers admit to as fruit and vegetable prices spike
text:
in brief A survey of over 2,500 shoppers found more than one in five are eating less fresh produce to save money.

Supply chain pressures have affected fuel and freight expenses, with farmers also spending more on fertiliser, driving up prices.

Australians are cutting their fresh produce spending by more than a quarter as the cost of living crunch changes how they shop — with some admitting to removing broccoli stalks and others selecting cheaper varieties at self-serve checkouts.

New research from price comparison site Canstar, released on Tuesday morning, found that the average amount Australians spend on fresh fruit and vegetables each week has fallen by 26 per cent, from $43 in 2025 to $32 this year.

The survey of over 2,500 shoppers also found more than one in five — 22 per cent — are eating less fresh produce to save money.

Previous Canstar research from July found that a grocery shop of staple items was around 8.5 per cent more expensive than in March 2025, with essentials like eggs and milk seeing some of the sharpest increases.

Supply chain pressures have affected fuel and freight expenses, with farmers also spending more on fertiliser, driving up prices at the checkout.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

For some households, cutting costs means changing what they buy rather than simply buying less – but some of the cost-cutting measures are more unusual.

How are Australians reducing fruit and veg costs?

The findings suggest rising grocery costs are affecting not only how much Australians spend, but also what they eat and how they shop.

Canstar consumer expert Eden Radford told SBS News the figures show households are actively looking for ways to manage rising grocery bills.

"Cost of living pressures are reshaping how Australians shop for fresh produce," Radford said.

"It's evident that shoppers are trying all approaches to stretch their dollar further."

More than four in 10 shoppers, or 42 per cent, said they are buying only what they can afford rather than what they would ideally like to eat, according to Canstar.

A third are opting for so-called "ugly" fruit and vegetables, while a quarter are buying more frozen produce because it is cheaper.

Another 23 per cent said they are buying more frozen produce to avoid fresh food going to waste.

Source: SBS News

Others are resorting to unorthodox methods to save.

Twelve per cent of shoppers said they have reduced the weight of their purchases — including by removing parts of produce such as broccoli stalks.

READ MORE Strait of Hormuz grinds to a halt as US threatens Iran

And 6 per cent admitted to deliberately selecting a cheaper option at self-service checkouts, such as entering a lower-priced variety of produce rather than the item they had actually chosen. For example, brown mushrooms attract a higher price than the regular, white button variety.

Radford explained that shoppers are becoming more "savvy" out of necessity, and half are splitting their time between multiple stores.

Opting for cheaper, frozen vegetables, which have a longer shelf life, and buying produce when it's in season are both ways Australians are cutting back on spending.

"The price of a punnet of apples can go up and down by a few dollars based on which months you're buying it in, and shoppers are paying attention," she said.

Quality over price?

The Canstar survey also analysed the biggest driver of consumer satisfaction, with freshness of produce found to be the main factor, followed by value for money and variety and presentation last.

Supermarket chain IGA ranked highest in consumer satisfaction for fruit and veg, overtaking the comparatively cheaper Aldi chain, which has held top spot for the past five years. This could suggest that shoppers surveyed this year are prioritising quality over price.

"Different supermarkets deliver better than others in different ways, and depending on a shopper's priority, they're not afraid to move around," Radford said.

Canstar data suggests that 47 per cent of shoppers buy their groceries from two different supermarkets, while 18 per cent visit three or more.

Food prices 'at risk'

Betashares chief economist David Bassanese told SBS News that elevated prices show no sign of slowing down as the economy endures multiple "shocks".

Energy prices have increased costs for deliveries, and warmer, drier seasons are also disrupting food supply, he explained.

The cost of operations for supermarkets has also increased due to the increase in the minimum wage earlier this year.

"Food prices are at risk from these factors," he said.

"The only way we are going to be able to deal with these pressures is to unfortunately slow the economy and reduce people's spending power."

But he said there's "no easy answer" to bringing prices down.

title: If Australia has a housing shortage, why are so many home builders collapsing?
text:
In brief Thousands of Australian construction companies collapsed in the last financial year.

They made up a quarter of all insolvencies nationally, despite ongoing demand for new homes.

Across Australia, thousands of people are waiting to find out if their homes will be built, after several separate construction company collapses.

By far the biggest of those recent collapses has been the Bathla Group, a Sydney developer that’s been one of Australia’s largest affordable home builders.

Owing about $3.4 billion to private lenders, Bathla's voluntary administration has thrown the construction of more than 2,000 apartments into limbo, while jeopardising a further pipeline of 14,000 homes.

More builders going bust since COVID

Figures released last week show 3,472 Australian construction companies went bust in the financial year to 30 June 2026: one in four (24.5 per cent) of all company insolvencies nationally.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The only good news? The number of builder insolvencies was slightly down for the first time since a steep rise began during COVID.

However, our research has found insolvencies in the construction sector remain consistently higher than in other industries. That makes it harder to build the housing we need.

Australia is falling further behind in meeting the federal government’s 1.2 million new homes goal by 2029.

Official forecasts released last month indicate the target won’t be met until December 2030. NSW — Australia’s largest housing market — may not meet its targets until March 2032, three years late on a five-year target.

There's no shortage of demand for new homes. What we lack is a construction system capable of delivering them reliably, sustainably and at scale.

Bathla's financial ripple effects

On Monday, more than 200 of Bathla’s 350 staff were stood down as the administrator continues to work on a rescue deal.

While most of its building projects are in western Sydney, Bathla's collapse is being watched around Australia because of its wider financial impacts.

READ MORE Homebuyers left in the dark as embattled property developer Bathla confirms major lay-offs

Like any company collapse, there are specific circumstances involved in Bathla's current woes. Its business model relied on high volumes of low-cost building.

The NSW building regulator has also conducted more than 40 inspections of Bathla sites in recent months, and ordered the builder to fix serious defects in one major development.

Bathla may have taken as many as 1,000 deposits from buyers for homes now stalled. But home buyers aren't the only people affected.

'Troubling developments' in private credit

As well as owing money to subcontractors, Bathla owes money to a long list of non‑bank lenders — also known as private credit firms.

This reflects the construction industry's heavy reliance on alternative finance, because banks have reduced their exposure to riskier lending.

On Friday, Australian Securities and Investments Commission chair Sarah Court said the corporate watchdog was closely following "several troubling developments in the private credit sector, most notably with the recent collapse of Bathla".

Court pointed out that many Australians are exposed to private credit through their superannuation funds — meaning "this is not some peripheral issue".

The perfect storm hitting builders

Bathla is not an isolated case. The wider construction industry is under strain, with higher costs, thinner profit margins and rising risks.

Figures released last month show house construction costs are now 51 per cent higher than before COVID.

For builders with slim profit margins, the rise in costs can make some projects uneconomic.

With costs rising unpredictably, builders locked into fixed-price contracts are absorbing losses they cannot sustain. This was a major driver of the spike in builder insolvencies during COVID.

Falling house prices and poor market sentiment mean some projects no longer stack up financially.

Many investors and buyers are spooked by three interest rate rises this year, higher costs, and recent federal budget changes to housing tax concessions that have made housing less attractive to investors. The prospect of further interest rate increases is also likely to see projects stalled, as the market waits for conditions to improve.

Then there are ongoing shortages of tradespeople. On top of those, home builders are now competing with data centre builders for tradies, which has driven up salaries.

Little wonder construction insolvencies have risen back to pre-COVID levels, despite strong demand for housing.

Structural change is needed

Governments can’t fix all the problems we face, such as price hikes driven by the Middle East war.

But federal, state and local governments are increasingly recognising their role in creating structural barriers to building more homes.

A Productivity Commission draft report released in July identified many of the problems we need to address, including restrictive land-use regulation, slow and inconsistent approvals, poor coordination on key infrastructure, and complex regulation. These all increase costs and delays.

Our 2025 report showed over-regulation is particularly hard on small builders, who struggle to comply with overlapping national, state and local requirements. That matters because our research also showed almost two-thirds (63 per cent) of building company collapses were concentrated among small builders.

The National Construction Code is another challenge. Even with some states deferring 2025 code changes, the national rules remain complex and frequently updated – again, making compliance difficult for small builders.

What’s safer than houses?

Some builders are responding by pivoting to infrastructure and commercial projects, such as Victoria’s Big Housing Build or Queensland’s Olympics construction projects. These can offer more manageable terms and less exposure to market volatility.

Good builders can pick and choose their work. Right now, housing is the riskiest option on the table.

Until that changes, we’re likely to see more Australian builders moving away from creating the homes we urgently need — along with more headlines about another builder going bust.

Lyndall Bryant is a senior lecturer at Queensland University of Technology's Centre for Justice in the School of Econmics and Finance. She is doing funded research on financial risks in housing supply for the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute. She has also received past funding from the Building 4.0 Cooperative Research Council grant — an industry-led research initiative co-funded by the Australian government. title: Austria's headscarf ban for under-14s faces first test as new school year starts
text:
Key Points Muslim students under the age of 14 will be prevented from wearing headscarves in Austrian schools.

Rights groups and experts say the move risks deepening social divisions amid high anti-immigration sentiment.

Austria's ban on headscarves for under-14s faces an initial test as schools reopen in Vienna and other ‌states, with groups including the country's main Muslim organisation denouncing it as discriminatory and legal ‌challenges likely.

Austria's centrist ruling coalition of three parties, led by the conservative Austrian People's Party, proposed the ban in schools, arguing ‌it was acting to protect girls' freedom.

The legislation was passed in parliament in December with the support of the far-right Freedom Party. Only the smallest party in parliament, the left-wing Greens, opposed it.

The group that formally represents Austria's Muslims, the Islamic ‌Religious Community in ‌Austria (IGGO), has ⁠said the move was an infringement of fundamental rights, pledging to fight it before the Constitutional Court, which rejected challenges in July because the legislation had not yet gone into force.

The court ruled in 2020 that a previous ban, which applied to under-10s in schools, was illegal because it discriminated against Muslims ⁠and the state had a duty ‌to be religiously neutral.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Going against that principle requires special justification, it held.

Asked by national broadcaster ORF if ‌the court would overturn the new ban, education minister Christoph Wiederkehr said: "You can never be completely certain".

"We in the government carried out very intensive consultations and we in the education ministry tried very hard to write a law that complies with the constitution," Wiederkehr said.

Left-wing ‌pupils' organisations have called for protests. The new school year starts on Monday in three of Austria's nine states — Vienna, the surrounding state of Lower Austria, and Burgenland, all in the east — with the rest following next week.

The legislation stipulates a school must hold discussions with any pupil defying the ban, after which a fine of ⁠between 150 and 800 euros ($A243 to $A1,290) can be imposed.

'It's my decision'

With anti-immigration sentiment running high in Austria, the government had argued the law was aimed at protecting girls from "oppression".

But rights groups and experts say it risked deepening social divisions.

"It's my decision... No one can force me to wear a headscarf, and no one can force me to take it off," a 12-year-old student told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency at a protest against the ban in Vienna earlier this year.

Malika Mataeva, co-founder of the Muslim Women Network, decried "years of systematic, deeply rooted racism in Austria" at the time.

Roughly eight percent of Austria's nine million residents are Muslim, according to 2021 government statistics.

In March, Austria's education ministry sent out information to all schools on how to enforce the new law.

It contained illustrations of different Islamic head coverings.

"Every teacher who observes a violation must instruct the student to remove her headscarf. If she does not immediately comply, the teacher must report the violation to the school administration without delay," the instructions state.

"The school administration must immediately hold a meeting with the student and her legal guardians."

Failure to report those in violation of the law could also have "legal consequences" for teachers and school managements, the instructions warn.

One Vienna schoolteacher, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told AFP she was not planning to enforce the law.

"It's a populist measure" that fails to address "the real problem when parents of any religion use violence or psychological violence against children," she said.
