title: 'Probably feel worse, not better': Government proposal to change daily habit questioned
text:
In Brief The government is set to unveil new draft laws this week allowing users to opt out of social media algorithms.

But the execution will be key to people adopting it, experts say.

Your morning scroll could look very different under new draft laws from the federal government, which plan to give social media users the chance to switch off the algorithm shaping their feed.

An exposure draft of the long-awaited Digital Duty of Care is expected this week, which will put the onus on platforms to risk-test their products before rolling them out — with one proposed measure forcing social media giants to let users opt out of the recommender systems that decide what content they see.

But the plan is already facing pushback, with the Coalition and the Greens both flagging problems with the approach from opposite directions, while other experts have welcomed the change but say the devil is in the detail.

What's the government proposing?

Under the new laws, platforms will be required to offer an opt-out from algorithm-driven feeds.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Communications Minister Anika Wells says the goal is choice, not a ban on algorithms altogether.

"A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment that they get out of it or the utility that they get out of it," she told ABC News on Monday morning, adding that big tech should "offer them the choice in the first place" and "respect that choice".

Communications Minister Anika Wells said the goal wasn't to ban algorithms entirely, but to give users a choice to opt-out. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Companies could be fined up to $109.2 million for breaching the wider duty of care laws, which also require platforms to actively mitigate risks on their platforms.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan argued the reform is redundant.

"People can already opt out of algorithms in their accounts. Why do we need the government here?" he said on Monday morning, accusing the government of using the policy to "silence people" from engaging with content critical of it.

But existing options to opt out of the algorithm are harder to use than that suggests.

"It's not true that you can opt out of recommender systems on all platforms," Tama Leaver, professor of internet studies at Curtin University, told SBS News.

On Instagram for instance, users can toggle to a followers-only feed, he says, but it snaps back to the algorithmic version every time they log back in. A different setting that lets users snooze certain personalised content resets every month.

Where opt-outs do exist, he said they're often "buried" in menus, requiring a "deep dive" to find them.

How would it work?

That's the big question — and one that can't clearly be answered yet.

Leaver said the execution would determine whether anyone bothers to opt out.

"The question of what you will get instead is the thing that will decide whether people will try this out or not," Leaver told SBS News.

He said a return to a reverse chronological feed — the model Instagram launched with — would show only posts from accounts you follow, in the order they were posted, and you could reach the end of your feed — rather than today's endless scroll.

But that's a harder sell than it sounds. Fewer people post to their main feeds these days, Leaver noted, which could mean an alternative execution of serving videos based on generic identifiers, like gender.

"Does it mean going back to the reverse chronological feed of 2012, or does it mean that you get a recommender algorithm that's just not personalised to you, but to the general population?" he said.

"For many people, that would probably feel worse, not better."

There's also the question of which algorithm gets switched off.

Platforms such as Instagram run several at once — separate systems sort the main feed, Stories and Reels — so an opt-out would need to specify whether it's turning off one, or all three.

On TikTok, Leaver noted, the algorithm-based For You page is its key product.

"That's the only place the vast majority of people go," he said. "So there are some big architectural questions here."

Leaver said all of this is guesswork until the government releases the actual details.

Will it solve the problem?

Unlike Australia's under-16s social media ban, the new laws wouldn't explicitly target young people —it would apply to everyone.

Experts say that's because the reform is trying to solve two separate problems: the addictive design of social media, and young people's exposure to extremist content.

READ MORE This toxic online world has an unstoppable pull. That may be about to change

On the first, Swinburne University media expert Belinda Barnet says it would help.

"It's actually not that radical. It's just kind of a move back in time to before all of these automated, essentially AI algorithms," Barnet told the Australian Associated Press.

"It's not going to get rid of predators or the many other issues that they could encounter on digital platforms ... this is really just removing one of the addictive elements from it."

READ MORE The 'harmful' online rabbit hole finding teens within minutes

On the second — boys and young men being funnelled toward extremist and misogynistic content — Leaver says it comes down entirely to which version of "opt-out" the legislation delivers.

"I think it will be successful if the option that is presented is to go to a reverse chronological feed," he said. "If this is simply the option to go to a recommender-driven feed that is not based on you, then I think the change is probably pointless and may in fact make it worse."

Outcry like protesting seatbelts, health minister says

Already, the government is facing political backlash.

The Greens said they were awaiting the draft legislation before deciding their approach, but Senator Sarah Hanson-Young has proposed her own bill, calling for an algorithm opt-out to be the default setting.

The Coalition is also yet to establish its position on the proposal, but Opposition leader Angus Taylor on Sunday expressed doubts about Labor's plan.

He said parents should have more control over what their children could see on social media, but he was "deeply sceptical" that the proposal wasn't an attempt to censor people's feeds.

Taylor accused Labor of butchering the already implemented under-16s social media ban — which the Coalition supported — adding the government should focus on fixing that policy.

Health Minister Mark Butler said the reforms were crucial to keeping people safe online.

"The idea is that this is some censorship or infringement of civil liberties almost harks back to the days of the 1970s when people were protesting about seatbelts being introduced to cars," he told ABC Radio.

"It's pretty unremarkable really to expect that big companies have a duty of care not to harm Australian citizens, particularly, frankly, young Australians.

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: Homebuyers left in the dark as embattled property developer Bathla confirms major lay-offs
text:
in brief More than 210 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning.

Homebuyers who bought off-the-plan have been left in the dark, uncertain when, or if, their properties will be completed.

Property developer Bathla Group has stood down almost two-thirds of its workforce following its entry into voluntary administration earlier this year.

About 213 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning, and construction on several projects has halted as the embattled firm clings to life.

Bathla is one of Sydney's largest residential developers, with 45 projects under construction.

Administrators said they had secured short-term funding to keep some of the firm's projects going.

Insolvency adviser Teneo announced it had secured the funding through five lenders linked to the projects, but the amounts and participants were kept confidential.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Administrator Stephen Longley said the funding would enable Bathla Group to maintain limited operations for a further two weeks while longer-term solutions were explored.

"Our immediate priority has been to secure sufficient short-term funding to maintain a minimum viable operating structure," he said.

"The arrangements agreed allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package.

"Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction. We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements."

NSW premier reacts

NSW Premier Chris Minns said the government was talking with administrators, but defended not spending public money bailing out the Sydney-based business.

Minns described Bathla's corporate structure as strange and highly reliant on debt from private lenders.

"I can't just hand money over to an administrator, particularly when the finances of this particular firm are so opaque and difficult to decipher," Minns said.

"There's been a lot of commentary about the way this company ... was managed and run, particularly the enormous amount of debt it ran up.

"This is a very strange corporate structure involving a hell of a lot of debt, largely collected from private credit, not through the banks and traditional finances."

Figures presented to creditors put Bathla's total debt at $3.4 billion, including $3.08 billion to secured lenders, $130 million to unsecured lenders, $145 million to the tax office and $4 million to employees.

The home developer entered voluntary administration in late August after the NSW government declined to bail it out.

'Slow-moving trainwreck'

Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler said issues with Bathla were widely known and called the firm a "slow-moving trainwreck".

"I've had lots of contractors come to me since I retired as commissioner, saying they'd been approached by Bathla to come and actually finish or undertake projects for them," he told ABC TV.

"They said to me there was no way because they were such a difficult group to work with ... it was hard to get paid."

Chandler said those who bought an uncompleted Bathla home off the plan should be able to get their deposit back, because the money was supposed to have been held in trust.

"The people who will be most caught out here will be trade contractors and suppliers who haven't been paid, and some not paid for a very long time," he said.

According to the company's website, the group has 20,000 apartments and 7,000 dwellings in its delivery pipeline, comprising a significant share of the NSW government's target of 75,400 new homes a year for five years until 2029.

Homebuyers who bought off-the-plan have been left in the dark, uncertain when, or if, their properties will be completed, while contractors have been left scrambling to recoup debts.

Founded in NSW in 1997, Bathla is among a long list of Australian home developers that have recently entered voluntary administration or liquidation.

title: The $25,000 loss critics warn lies under One Nation's superannuation plan
text:
IN BRIEF Under a newly proposed One Nation policy, Australians could access their superannuation earlier and more easily.

For some Australians, opting into the scheme could mean they lose $25,000 from their retirement fund.

One Nation's plan to allow workers to extract part of their superannuation as take-home-pay could leave Australians poorer in retirement while charging future taxpayers more, experts and critics warn.

One Nation has proposed changes to superannuation that would allow workers paying rent or a mortgage to divert 3 per cent of their super payments straight to their wallet for up to three years — investing only 9 per cent instead of the current compulsory rate of 12 per cent.

Employers would still contribute 12 per cent, but the nominated super fund would invest only 9 per cent — paying out 3 per cent to the customer.

Payments would be taxed at the concessional rate of 15 per cent rather than the personal income tax rate.

Party leader Pauline Hanson said the policy would give households "breathing room" and would help people to buy groceries, power bills and the costs of raising a family.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"For a full-time worker earning about $90,500, that means around $2,300 a year after tax, or $44 a week, extra in their pocket," she said.

"For a working couple earning $168,000 between them, it is about $4,300 a year after tax, or $82 a week, back in the family budget.

"That's a real boost to help you pay the rent or the mortgage."

But the policy has been criticised for its potential impact on retirement, with some saying it could leave thousands worse off later in life.

READ MORE When should you be able to access your super? Battle lines are being drawn

Mardy Chiah, associate professor of finance at the University of Newcastle's School of Business, estimated that it would result in a loss of about $23,000 to $24,000 in invested income.

"If you're earning an average $90,000 salary, the 3 per cent would give you an extra $2,300 a year — which after three years would be $6,900," Chiah said, explaining the calculation.

"This policy essentially gives households more financial breathing room today in exchange for ... much less money invested for their retirement.

"The loss can be quite substantial. You're taking money away from your future self."

A similar loss was projected by the Super Members Council's analysis of the policy, which said a 30-year-old full-time worker on a salary of $90,500 who opts into One Nation's policy would be down $25,000 in retirement superannuation.

The same 30-year-old worker would lose over $18,000 in compounding interest by the time they reach the retirement age of 67.

Source: SBS News

Super Members Council CEO Misha Schubert said the scheme would damage a person's super and retirement and increase "inflation and interest rates — which would make cost-of-living pressures even worse".

"There are smarter and better ways to help Australians struggling with housing costs ... none of them involve telling Australians to raid their super and their futures."

Currently, the mandatory superannuation contribution rate is set at 12 per cent. Chiah warns investing only 9 per cent could compromise someone's ability to "retire comfortably" — and be a "liability for taxpayers".

"More people would likely have to access the age pension for their retirement, which means future taxpayers would be funding this policy."

Chiah believes the "preservation of a retirement fund" is crucial for all Australians, and interfering with investments should be a "last resort".

"It's really important that people understand that super is meant for your retirement ... if you retire at 67, you will need that money," he said.

READ MORE The $400k super line that could define how comfortable retirement is

The Australian Council of Trade Unions suggested there were better cost of living measures such as minimum wage rises, penalty rates and safer workplaces.

"It's typical that the only pay rise Pauline Hanson could imagine a worker deserving is one at the expense of their own retirement income," ACTU assistant secretary Joseph Mitchell said.

"Forget robbing Peter to pay Paul, this is robbing Peter to pay Peter."

'End of superannuation as we know it'

Treasurer Jim Chalmers warned One Nation's policy could "end superannuation as we know it".

"It's now beyond doubt that any Coalition government with One Nation in it will cut your super," he said during a doorstop interview at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday.

"By ending super as we know it, by making Australian workers poorer as a consequence ... this is exactly why One Nation poses an unacceptable and dangerous risk to Australian workers."

Hanson rejected Chalmers' comments, saying she's "not intending to shut super down".

"If it comes to a point of someone being out in the streets and living in a tent or on the cusp of losing their home, I would rather see them get that help and assistance that they need now, not later in life."

READ MORE Labor reveals super increase position amid 'predatory' practices crackdown

Nationals MP David Littleproud said the policy could see "unintended consequences" such as higher inflation.

"When you've got inflation out of control at the moment, and you fuel that with putting more money into the economy, the unintended consequence is that inflation will go up and interest rates will go up," he told News24 on Monday.

However, One Nation's treasury spokesperson Barnaby Joyce also told News24 the impact on inflation would be "undetectable" or "incredibly small".

"In the circumstances where you're tying the money up in a house payment, I can't see how the volume of money in the economy would be exacerbated that much," he said.

"If your rent payments are $600 a week, your rent payment would still be $600 a week and therefore the money that the person collecting the rent is getting is still $600 a week. If the money is going to your house payments, it's still the same.

"You could say that if the volume increases there is an inflationary aspect, that's a statement of fact. The proportion, I would say, would be incredibly small."

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume ridiculed the policy.

"This so far is nothing more than a headline," she told ABC News Breakfast.

"One Nation does have a bit of a habit of putting out a headline and putting out on details — they don't think this is a serious thing."

title: Qantas flight makes priority landing after engine issue sparks panic over New Zealand
text:
in brief Passengers described a terrifying ordeal after flames and loud bangs were seen coming from the left engine of the plane.

The Boeing 737 landed safely in Christchurch, where emergency crews were waiting.

Emergency services were called to the tarmac when a Qantas flight made a priority landing in Christchurch after an engine issue, which one passenger described as "traumatic".

Liza-Jayne Loch was returning home from a business trip to New Zealand when the Qantas flight ran into trouble.

The plane was climbing above the scenic South Island's mountain ranges on Saturday afternoon, bound for Sydney, when a bang shook the cabin.

A passenger seated nearest the left wing soon shouted, "the engine's on fire", Loch recalled, as the cabin lights began to flicker.

Footage recorded by a passenger and shared with AAP shows flames appearing to issue from the plane's left engine in a series of rapid bursts.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I was sitting on the left-hand side of the plane, and the flames were very, very visible," Loch said.

"There was a lot of screaming at the time."

As the plane continued to gain altitude, Loch tried to comfort herself by recalling that modern jets could land safely on a single engine.

"That's what I kept in my head, that we could actually fly on one engine," she said.

"But the flames kept coming and the noise kept coming."

QF122 suffered a suspected engine issue shortly after taking off from Queenstown on Saturday afternoon, before making a priority landing at Christchurch.

According to Flight Aware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after take-off, touching down shortly before 5pm local time.

The cause of the incident has yet to be determined, but Qantas sent two engineers to Christchurch on Sunday to investigate.

Both engines are thought to have remained in operation for the duration of the flight.

Loch said conditions soon stabilised after the initial shock, while cabin staff took pains to comfort passengers.

"The crew were all terribly, terribly calming," Loch said.

'Massive cheers'

Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac when the flight landed, and passengers were allowed to disembark as normal after a short wait.

"There were massive cheers when we landed," Loch said.

A Qantas spokesperson said the plane was believed to have suffered an engine issue and steps would be taken to support affected customers.

"Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely," they said.

"We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support."

Affected passengers were put up in a hotel near the Christchurch International Airport before being booked on a complimentary flight to Sydney on Sunday.

While the second flight went off without a hitch, Loch said nerves were still high.

"I cried getting off the plane when we landed in Sydney," Loch said.

"It was quite traumatic."

title: Labor urges Greens, Coalition to pass social media reforms after 'dawdling and delay'
text:
IN BRIEF Labor is urging the Senate to back reforms aimed at strengthening enforcement of the under-16 social media ban.

The government is also set to unveil draft reforms mandating the ability to opt out of social media algorithms.

Labor is urging the Greens and Coalition to pass laws that would strengthen the eSafety Commissioner's powers to gather information from social media companies and increase fines tech giants face for breaches of the teen social media ban.

When Labor introduced the bill in late June, Communications Minister Anika Wells said an eSafety investigation had suggested several major social media companies were exploiting loopholes in the law.

"The commissioner has found these companies adopting a number of dirty tricks to undermine Australia's law that are straight out of the big-tech playbook," Wells said at the time.

"It is clear ... that social media companies are deliberately failing to comply with our laws."

The bill would give the eSafety Commissioner enhanced information-gathering powers that Labor argues are necessary to ensure social media companies take 'reasonable steps' to prevent under-16s from creating or retaining social media accounts, as required under the ban.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In March-April, the eSafety Commissioner found 81.5 per cent of 10-15-year-olds were still using at least one age-restricted platform, a small decline from the 85.9 per cent it found before the ban came into effect on 10 December 2025.

However, the government has reported that more than five million social media accounts belonging to under-16s have been deleted, deactivated or restricted since the ban came into effect.

Meta — the parent company of Facebook and Instagram — said in mid-August that it had taken down more than 750,000 accounts and said those numbers would "continue to grow".

"We share the Australian government's goal of ensuring young people have safe, age-appropriate experiences online, and we are meeting our obligations under the law," the company added in a statement released at the time.

'Put politics to the side'

In early July, Greens and Coalition senators voted to send Labor's bill to a Senate inquiry, which eight weeks later recommended the reforms be adopted.

Wells said on Sunday that the decision to send the bill to an inquiry was "the kind of dawdling and delay that has enabled social media companies to get away with harming our kids for so long".

"We have to put politics to the side and pass this bill this week, so the eSafety Commissioner can hold social media companies accountable," she said.

READ MORE This toxic online world has an unstoppable pull. That may be about to change

When voting to refer the bill to the inquiry, Liberal Senator Sarah Henderson accused Labor of trying to "ram through" the new powers without proper scrutiny.

"Rather than Anika Wells' mad scramble to fix her broken ban, much more needs to be done to protect children online," she said.

The Greens also said Labor needed to go further.

"We need to urgently regulate algorithms, and make it clear that social media companies are responsible for the extreme harm their platforms perpetrate," the left-wing party said in its additional comments to the inquiry report.

'Digital duty of care' reforms

The regulation of social media algorithms is an issue that will soon come to the fore in Canberra, with Labor set to release details of proposed laws that would force tech giants to give users the ability to opt out of algorithms.

An exposure draft of the so-called 'digital duty of care' reforms is expected to be released in the coming sitting fortnight.

It would put the onus on social media companies to mitigate risk on their platforms, including actively removing illegal or harmful content.

The option to opt out of algorithms would be mandatory, giving users the choice to take their social media feeds back to the friends-only content they once were.

READ MORE The 'harmful' online rabbit hole finding teens within minutes

Several areas are expected to be identified as off-limits to minors due to the potential for psychological harm, including content that promoted harmful body image.

The changes would prevent boys from being bombarded with violent and misogynistic material, Labor's Matt Thistlethwaite told News24's Sunday Agenda program.

"Many Australian parents have said that they're concerned about their children being exposed to this material," he said.

"We think that the platforms have a responsibility to try and keep young Australian kids safe.

Greens call for larger fines

However, the measures could struggle to pass the Senate in their current form, with Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young saying proposed fines of up to $100 million for breaching the laws were insufficient.

Hanson-Young told reporters that tech companies would see such fines as part of the cost of doing business, and called for penalties to be calculated based on each firm's global profits.

"The power of big tech is so immense and you can't take them on and hit them at their business model with half-baked measures," she said.

READ MORE A landmark US deal could change social media forever

"The government's really going to have to toughen up.

"Either take on big tech properly, or you'll end up putting in place a scheme that really does bugger all."

The Greens are awaiting details of the exposure draft before deciding how to vote, while Senator Hanson-Young has proposed her own bill, calling for an algorithm opt-out to be the default setting.

That measure has been the focus of a campaign by Teach Us Consent's Fix Our Feeds, which has been pushing for linear social media feeds to be the default option.

In a linear social media feed, content would appear in chronological order, with users only seeing posts from people or accounts they have chosen to follow.

The organisation's founder, Chanel Contos, recently said an algorithm opt-out was a good first step, but the measure did not go far enough to stop boys and young men being exposed to harmful content.

"It would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," she told the National Press Club in early September.

Coalition says govt should focus on fixing ban

The Opposition is also yet to establish its position on the proposal, but leader Angus Taylor on Sunday expressed doubts about Labor's plan.

He said parents should have more control over what their children could see on social media, but he was "deeply sceptical" that the proposal wasn't an attempt to censor people's feeds.

Taylor accused Labor of butchering the already implemented under-16s social media ban, which the Coalition supported, adding the government should focus on fixing that policy.

"The government should be focused on that because it's not working," he said.

"So then going off and starting on some other thing ... there's good reason to be sceptical about that."

title: 'Titan of Australian sport': Boxer Tony Mundine honoured at heartfelt Redfern memorial
text:
IN BRIEF Australian boxing great, Tony Mundine, passed away on 30 August from a heart attack.

Mundine remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions.

WARNING: This article contains the name and image of an Aboriginal person who has passed away.

Respected Bundjalung boxer Anthony 'Tony' Mundine OAM has been remembered as an "unwavering anchor" of strength and determination at an emotional ceremony in Sydney's Redfern.

Crowds gathered at Redfern Oval on Saturday morning to pay their respects to Mundine, who died from a heart attack on 30 August — aged 75.

His coffin was carried to a small stage — decorated with a large bouquet and the Aboriginal flag proudly draped across the top.

On the side, the dark wood was printed with a pair of boxing gloves and a gold rabbit, a nod to Mundine's loyal, lifelong love of the South Sydney Rabbitohs.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Bundjalung and Gadigal man Craig Madden, nephew to "Uncle Tony", welcomed guests to Country.

He recalled the life of a man who, at 15, came to Sydney to chase his dreams "into the ring".

Madden described Mundine as the "backbone" of their family.

"Steady, loyal and always there when you needed him. He was strong and staunch, yet humble, kind and generous beyond measure," he said.

"He always made room for a yarn and a laugh, or a quiet word when someone needed comfort."

"He was not a man who wasted words; the ones he shared carried wisdom, warmth and strength ... he shared lessons about life that stayed with you —leaving you feeling hopeful, grounded and ready to face what was to come next."

Tony Mundine's commitment to community lasted his entire life. Supplied by the Mundine Family. Source: Supplied / The Mundine Family

Mundine's nephew, Matthew Mundine, delivered the eulogy.

He reflected on Mundine's "quiet resilience, unwavering integrity and deep strength of character" that saw him become a "titan of Australian sport".

Acknowledging the legend's achievements in the ring, Mundine Jr said his "greatest victory" was the establishment of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym and the Tony Mundine Hostel.

"He built far more than physical places — he built sanctuaries of hope," said Mundine Jr.

"For generations of community and young people, especially Aboriginal youth seeking direction, safe housing or a second chance, Tony offered a home away from home."

A "steady anchor", Mundine was a "deeply devoted" family man and a "loyal and steadfast" friend.

"Your fight may be done, but your victories are eternal — and your legacy will never fade."

Mundine's four children, Kelly, Natalie, Anthony and Kiah, also paid tribute to their father.

His youngest child, Kiah Tony Mundine Atkins, described her father as "positive, friendly, kind and happy", a man who "loved people" and deeply loved his grandchildren.

She recalled his cheekiness, his pride in his bright red car he constantly washed, and his funny sayings, "stone the crows, and everybody was a cowboy".

"Whenever I would ask my Dad, 'How are you, Dad?' He would say, 'I'm cruising like a butterfly'," she said.

"Keep cruising like a butterfly, Dad. I love you."

Mundine's eldest, Natalie Carr-Mundine, said her Dad had a special way of "touching people's lives".

"His legacy isn't measured by the titles he has won, or the fights he fought," she said.

"It's measured by the people he has inspired, and looking here today, he's inspired quite a lot of you."

Former boxer and Mundine's only son, Anthony Mundine Junior said he aspires to be like his father.

"If I can be half the man he was in his life, I'm doing alright," he said.

READ MORE Vale Tony Mundine, the champion who inspired generations

Four of Mundine's grandsons spoke, with Jade Mundine Atkins describing his Pop as their "world".

"I'm incredibly proud to be his grandson."

Family members, Lowanna Mundine and Birrpai Elder Uncle Heath Bugg also shared tributes alongside Nick Barnett, Mundine's closest friend of fifty years.

The memorial also heard from friends, colleagues and competitors from Mundine's boxing career, including ringside doctor Dr Lou Lewis, IBF World Super Featherweight Champion Barry Michael and boxing trainer and International Boxing Hall of Fame inductee Johnny Lewis.

Tribal Warrior CEO Shane Phillips shared reflections on the importance of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym for Redfern's Aboriginal community, and Aboriginal Hostels CEO Shane Hamilton and Liz Simpson, who has managed the Tony Mundine Hostel for almost two decades, spoke about its impact on young Aboriginal men.

A young Tony Mundine ahead of his 1974 fight against American Bennie Briscoe. Source: Getty / Universal / Corbis / VCG

'A proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil'

Born on 10 June 1951, Mundine was "a proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil" — a small community on Bundjalung Country near Grafton in northern NSW.

He moved to Redfern at 15-years-old, following his talent in rugby league. But it was training in Ern McQuillan's Newtown gym that turned him to boxing.

Over 15 years, Mundine won 80 out of 96 fights and secured two Commonwealth titles. He remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions: middleweight, light heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight

He cemented his status as a champion in 1974, when he challenged Argentina's Carlos Monzón for the WBA world middleweight title.

Mundine shared his gift, training others including his son Anthony Mundine Jr and grandson Rahim Mundine.

In 1986, he was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia for his dedication and service to the sport of boxing and Aboriginal youth.

"Whether it was at the many national events and gatherings, or on The Block in Redfern, Coluzzi's Café in Kings Cross or in our family homes, Tony gave so much of himself to others," his family said in a statement after his passing.

"His legacy will live on through the many people he encouraged, mentored and inspired throughout his life."

The eastern suburbs skyline would be dramatically transformed with high-rise towers as tall as 34 storeys under NSW government plans to add 9400 new homes. Draft plans revealed on Tuesday show varied building heights of 34 storeys around Edgecliff station and 32 storeys around a to-be-built Woollahra station as part of a state government plan to ramp up housing supply east of Sydney’s CBD. Aerial render of Woollahra and Edgecliff station upzoning. The draft plans also include seven new parks, nine kilometres of new walking and cycling connections and a new Woollahra local centre which the government has promised will create more jobs and provide local services. The new homes would be built over the next 20 years over 168 hectares of eastern suburbs land, with 40 per cent of new homes to be delivered within 200 metres of a train station, with the new Woollahra heavy rail station to open in 2029. The aim of the rezoning proposal is to enable private developers to build taller and more dense projects, and there won’t be any compulsory acquisition of land.

Spider-Man has overcome the Green Goblin, Doc Ock and Venom, but his latest triumph over Titanic could be his most memorable yet. Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which landed in theatres on July 31, has now sunk James Cameron’s beloved classic, shifting the 1997 film from the top five highest-grossing movies at the global box office. Titanic enjoyed a spot in the top five for nearly three decades, even topping the list for 12 years before being dethroned in 2010. Since then, Titanic has plunged further down the rankings, even with re-releases. Now, thanks to Spidey, it’s out of the top five entirely. Spider-Man: Brand New Day swung into the top five highest-grossing movies of all time, sinking Titanic along the way. Sony/AP Granted, this doesn’t take inflation into account. Most top five lists consider the actual money accumulated at the time each movie was released (as well as revenue from any re-releases). Movie tickets were far cheaper when Titanic hit screens, so more contemporary blockbusters are bound to earn more. On an inflation-adjusted list, classics such as Gone with the Wind, Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope and The Sound of Music would quickly climb the ranks. Regardless, with Titanic now off the top handful, which films remain? Here’s a rundown of the five films that have made the most money around the world.

Advertisement

5. Ne Zha 2 This Chinese fantasy animation is the highest-grossing non-English language film in history. It proved incredibly popular in China, becoming the first film ever to take more than $US1 billion ($1.38 billion) in a single territory. However, its popularity expanded far beyond China. In Australia, it made its debut as the third-highest ranking feature at the local box office. By its second weekend, it had made $5.22 million. Though much of Ne Zha 2’s success can be attributed to love for the original film, as well as its emotional depth in storytelling and stunning visual effects, there were also reports of the film being boosted by Chinese patriotism and a social media campaign. Fans encouraged others online to watch the film in cinemas multiple times. Chinese companies also got on board, including snacks manufacturer Weilong Food, which paused operations to take 900 of its employees to see the movie.

Advertisement

4. Avatar: The Way of Water Cameron blew audiences out of the water with Avatar in 2009, but his sequel to the sci-fi epic threw them right back into it. Avatar: The Way of Water once again lured people back to the cinema to see the awe-inspiring visuals on the biggest screen possible (and, of course, in 3D). Cameron even developed entirely new technology to record actors performing in live action underwater. The long-awaited sequel brought back fan favourites such as Zoe Saldaña and Sigourney Weaver, but it also introduced new major names such as Kate Winslet. Everything these actors’ characters did on screen, the actors actually performed in real life, with the crew logging about 200,000 hours of free-diving. Winslet even smashed Tom Cruise’s previous record for longest-held breath, and held hers for a staggering seven minutes and 14 seconds (Cruise held his breath for just over six minutes in Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation). This brought an incredible air of authenticity and craft to the film, which evidently generated significant word-of-mouth. 3. Spider-Man: Brand New Day

Advertisement

Tom Holland’s successful run as Peter Parker continued with Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which has just enjoyed its sixth consecutive weekend atop the global box office. The film, directed by Dustin Daniel Cretton, hearkened back to Spider-Man’s roots, dropping Parker into the streets of New York where small-time criminals run amok. This return clearly paid off – the movie is currently experiencing the longest stint at No.1 since Avatar: The Way of Water in 2022. And according to Variety, Cretton’s movie is also primed to overtake Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) as the highest-grossing movie of all time at the US box office. These figures helped the Marvel film to not only bump Titanic – a cinematic behemoth that had been in the top five for nearly as long as Holland has been alive – but it also completely re-shuffled the list by overtaking both Ne Zha 2 and the Avatar sequel. 2. Avengers: Endgame

Advertisement

Avengers: Endgame was the finale to end all finales. After about 23 Marvel films, the Infinity Saga wrapped up with this behemoth of a blockbuster, one that brought some of the most famous superheroes – including Captain America and the Hulk – against a truly remarkable villain, Thanos. The stakes could not have been higher, as major names within the Marvel Cinematic Universe were snuffed out, and the fate of half of humanity lay in the hands of those who remained. Of course people wanted to see this on the big screen. Endgame may even rise further up the box office ranks, given it’s to be re-released this month ahead of the release of Avengers: Doomsday in December. 1. Avatar Cameron’s Titanic may have been knocked from the top, but the renowned director still claims two of the coveted spots, including No.1.

Advertisement

Avatar fundamentally changed cinema in 2009. It pioneered advanced motion capture and revolutionised 3D technology, attracting audiences for the visual spectacle alone. This earned it a best picture nomination at the Academy Awards. While it may not have won in that category, it did pick up Oscars for best cinematography, visual effects and art direction. The film enjoyed the top spot for about a decade before being briefly surpassed by Endgame in 2019. However, an Avatar re-release in China the following year reversed that, and it has remained the world’s highest-grossing movie since. What about Star Wars?! None of the Star Wars films are currently in the top five (though if these lists accounted for inflation, Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope likely would). title: Fighting the bully: Canada throws a punch back at Trump
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyTrade wars Opinion Fighting the bully: Canada throws a punch back at Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 8, 2026 — 11:59am

September 8, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Canada’s Mark Carney has risked an escalation in trade hostilities with the US by following through with his foreshadowed retaliatory tariffs on US imports. Just after midnight on Monday, Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on about $US20 billion ($28 billion) of US exports went live, making Canada, with China, the only significant economies willing to stand up to Donald Trump’s trade bullying. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office last year. AP Photo/Evan Vucci The tariffs are a response to a similar dollar amount of new tariffs on Canada’s exports to the US that the Trump administration imposed last month after talks between the countries – held against the backdrop of Trump’s threat of those tariffs unless Canada made a range of trade concessions – broke down. While willing to accept some duties and to tighten rules of origin that might have shifted more of the North American auto industry supply chain across the border into the US, last-minute demands from the US negotiators – abolishing Canadian French language local content rules and quotas, exclusive access to Canada’s minerals and restrictions on its ability to sign trade deals with other countries – caused Carney to end the negotiations.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump would plunge the US into crisis if he carried out his latest bizarre threat Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The US proceeded with its new tariffs on Canadian autos, dairy, alcohol, metals and consumer goods and now Canada has matched them on a dollar-for-dollar basis, targeting US apparel, timber, steel and aluminium, agricultural equipment, appliances, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics. Both countries had pre-existing tariffs, dating back to Trump’s initial declaration of a trade war on the rest of the world last year, his singling out (absurdly) Canada for its alleged role in fentanyl exports to the US and, more recently, a 10 per cent rate (along with much of the rest of the world) for its claimed failure to do enough to halt imports of goods made with forced labour. Canada had responded to the earliest of those tariffs with duties of its own, but the effective rate on US imports was only just above one per cent. With this week’s counter tariffs, it is now closer to 4 per cent. The effective rate of the tariffs on Canadian imports to the US was around 3 per cent before the recent changes. It’s now closer to 6 per cent. Carney’s willingness to stand up to the US is brave, bordering on foolhardy, given that nearly 70 per cent of Canada’s exports go to the US and that he doesn’t have the rare earths monopoly that China used to force Trump to back away from his direst trade threats to its economy.

Advertisement

There is some shelter from the United States-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement (USMCA), although that hasn’t stopped Trump from targeting Canada (or Mexico) with tariffs so far. Trump has been trying to use the threat of walking away from the USMCA (which he negotiated in his first term) as leverage to force more trade concessions from Canada and Mexico (although America’s withdrawal from the USMCA would take a decade), with Mexico more willing than Canada to do a new deal. Canada is standing up for itself, but almost 70 per cent of the country’s exports go to the US. Getty Images While Canada’s retaliation might provoke even stronger action from the US – Trump has threatened more tariffs and even (along with some other major US trading partners) the end of all trade – the three economies within the USMCA are highly integrated. Canada might be harmed more, but the US would also suffer self-harm if it responds to Canada’s new tariffs by raising its own.

Advertisement

By far the largest of Canada’s exports to the US are oil and refined products. It accounts for about 60 per cent of America’s oil imports. Because the oil is extracted from oil sands and is heavy, viscous and contains sulfur and metals, it requires specialised refining. Refineries in Texas and Louisiana process the imported oil. Related Article Analysis

US politics Trump’s weekend of trolling can’t paper over his political problems Trump hasn’t included Canadian oil, yet, in his list of sanctioned products. That would be self-destructive. Canada is, however, trying to diversify the customer base for its oil (and protect itself from the threat that America might displace its exports with similarly heavy Venezuelan crude) by planning to build a pipeline from its oil fields to the Pacific coast that would give it access to the Asian market. The Canadian and US auto and auto parts industries are closely entwined – auto parts can cross the border several times (and be charged duties each time) before vehicles are fully built – so tariff disruption will hurt both economies and their US company-dominated auto industries.

Advertisement

Last year Canada exported $US9.9 billion of aluminium and aluminium products to the US, for use in the auto industry, in cans, construction and a raft of other purposes. The US gets about 70 per cent of its imported primary aluminium from Canada and nearly 60 per cent of all its aluminium and aluminium products imports. The US aluminium industry has shrunk over decades, with some of the major US producers, like Alcoa, shifting their operations to Canada, with his vast hydroelectric power resources that provide cheap electricity to an exceptionally energy-intensive sector. Canada might be harmed more, but the US would also suffer self-harm if it responds to Canada’s new tariffs by raising its own. Trump might want to use tariffs to force companies to reshore activities to the US, but the US grid doesn’t produce electricity cheaply or reliably enough (and Trump is trying to stifle renewable sources) to compete with Canada. If Trump does escalate, Canada does have options that would hurt the US, create supply shortages and raise costs for US businesses and prices for US consumers.

Advertisement

While Canada and Canadians would also suffer – unlike Trump, some in his administration and many of his MAGA supporters, they understand how tariffs work and who pays the duties – they appear prepared to accept that as the price of sovereignty. Trump’s continued rumblings about the “51st state” have drawn Canadians together in their support for Carney and his response. Carney has also been busy since winning his office in March last year, negotiating a raft of trade agreements with other countries to try to diversify his economy away from its over-reliance on the US. That, no doubt, is why Trump’s negotiators tried to restrict its ability to do trade deals with third parties. Loading Thus, in the longer term, Trump’s ill-conceived trade assault on America’s closest ally and trading partner is likely – as is the case with other allies of long-standing – to lead to a fundamental change and distancing in the economic and political relationships between the countries.

Advertisement

Trump isn’t helping to lower the temperature with his continuing threats and juvenile social media posts, including one very recently which depicts Trump skating on ice, dressed in full ice hockey gear, savagely beating Carney with a hockey stick. Related Article Trump diplomacy Hegseth enrages Canada by mocking appearance of female military cadets Trump, of course, has never been seen on skates of any kind, while Carney was a very active and competitive ice hockey player in his youth, including a stint as the reserve goalkeeper for Harvard’s team. Trump’s post is rightly being criticised, and ridiculed. Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America, continuing to post maps of the United States that include Canada as a state and referring to Carney as “governor”, aren’t going to shift the increasingly anti-American sentiment in Canada. title: Incredible pics of car swallowed by sinkhole
text:
A driver had a lucky escape after their car dropped into a sinkhole in the early hours of the morning.

A Toyota Corolla was driving through floodwater along The Bridgeway at Canning Vale, in Perth's southeast, when their car became trapped just before 4am on Tuesday.

A Water Corporation spokesman said the sinkhole was caused by a burst water main overnight.

A Water Corporation spokesman said a burst water main caused flooding on the road. Picture: Facebook

"The driver was uninjured and able to safely exit the car," a spokesman said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Maintenance crews were at the scene within 30 minutes and isolated the main.

Work is now under way to remove the vehicle and make repairs.

The driver managed to escape their vehicle uninjured. Picture: Facebook

About 10 homes are without water and drivers are being urged to avoid the area while work is carried out to fix the sinkhole.

"Residents may notice discoloured water as repairs progress," a spokesman said.

"We wish to apologise for any disruption caused and thank residents for their patience as crews work to complete repairs."

title: ‘Global reckoning’: Labor’s next big social media crackdown
text:
A "global reckoning" is coming for big tech as Anthony Albanese announces the government's long-awaited digital duty of care.

Addressing the media in announcing the draft legislation on Tuesday, the Prime Minister said his government was acting on algorithms with its "my feed, by way" initiative.

The long-awaited digital duty of care laws aims to give users more control over the algorithms – the systems that shape what people see online.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

That often translates into emotionally and politically charged content on social media designed to keep people scrolling for longer, which radicalisation experts warn is driving people to extreme views.

"We'll require social media platforms provide user empowerment tools that give people over the age of 16 genuine and enduring choice about what they see in their feeds," Mr Albanese said.

Mr Albanese announced draft legislation for the long-awaited digital duty of care on Tuesday. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

"We have an opportunity to shape technology for the better rather than let it shape us. That is what our reforms are all about."

Under the reforms, social media platforms will be required to send a notification to new and existing users offering them a "choice over their default feed".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Social media users can choose to "opt in" to having their default feed include personalised content recommended by the algorithm, or they can "opt out" of personally recommended content and "see the friends and creators they choose to follow".

"If people want to doom scroll … that's up to them," Mr Albanese said.

"But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them with the opportunity."

Mr Albanese denied the reforms were about giving the government control.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said tech companies 'can still move fast, but they will no longer be able to break things'. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

"It's about giving people control. It's about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online through our digital duty of care," Mr Albanese said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The reforms will require platforms protect children from harmful content, including content promoting eating disorders and pornography.

It will also empower eSafety to issue removal notices for so-called nudify apps "and streamline the child cyber-bullying and adult cyber abuse schemes".

Penalties will also be bolstered to $100m.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said tech companies "can still move fast, but they will no longer be able to break things".

"There is a global reckoning coming for big tech," she said.

"With our digital duty of care we are taking the next step forward by requiring tech companies take responsibility for the harms that their products, tools and features are causing."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Pressed on whether the proposal was for either an opt-in or opt-out algorithm, Ms Wells said tech companies would need to allow users to choose their feed.

Teach Us Consent founder Chanel Contos said the reforms were 'a great first step'. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

"What this will look like in real life as a user is that the platform will have to offer you the option: 'What would you like your default primary feed to be? Would you like it to be the algorithm, or would you like it to be your following feed?" she said.

"So, the friends that you follow, the content creators that you choose to follow, you as a user will have to be offered that choice.

"Then, obviously, you'll have the ability to make that choice over and over, as much as you want to change your mind through the platform."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Albanese was flanked by advocates of reform to social media, including Chanel Contos' Teach Us Consent and proponents of the News Corp Australia's Let Them Be Kids campaign.

"This is an example of change from the bottom up. My government listening and acting," he said.

Teach Us Consent founder Chanel Contos said the reforms were "a great first step".

"It shows the government has heard what Australians have been telling us for months. We demand and deserve control over what we see online," she said.

"We're looking forward to working closely with the government to ensure this commitment holds up in the drafting."

Allegra Spender denied algorithm options were a freedom of speech issue. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

The Greens have indicated they would not give the government a "blank cheque".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

During a party room briefing, the minor party indicated it would be looking at the legislation "very carefully" to make sure it "actually does what it needs to do".

The party could seek to have the Bill referred to a Senate inquiry, as was done with Labor's legislation to bolster the under-16s social media ban.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce said he was nervous about the legislation in the minutes before it was announced, warning of "socialist censorship".

"I know what they're up to, this is censorship," he told News24.

Mr Joyce linked the looming measures to One Nation's win in the Secret Harbour by-election in Western Australia, which he said Labor believed was connected to "malfeasance in the social media process".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The thing about this socialist crowd is they lie," he said.

"So, when they say things, you say, why would I believe that? You also said you weren't going to change the capital gains tax."

'Conflated'

On Tuesday, Community First Australia MP Allegra Spender said attempts to give Australians more control over their social media feeds were being "conflated" with concerns about freedom of speech.

"What we're trying to do and what I think we should do here is give people the choice about whether they see content that they already follow, like their friends and groups they already follow, or they see content which is driven by the algorithm," she told News24.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I can't see how anyone can make an argument that you're impinging people's free speech or you're censoring them by giving them more choice about the content they see.

"If you start with the sort of vanilla version, and then you get to choose to opt in, the social media companies will want to make the option attractive.

Communications Minister Anika Wells is expected to unveil draft legislation. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman.

"But, they will still have to provide a decent opt-out option."

Ms Spender said giving Australians more control over the algorithm was "not going to fix all issues, but it's a starting point".

Asked whether she was concerned that it would be up to the government of the day to determine what is shown on people's feeds, Ms Spender said she was "very cautious" and would need to look at the legislation carefully.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She said it was important that Australian's views were "not being silenced".

"I think this is where we have to be pretty careful in relation to free speech … but, I will say, in my community, what we are seeing is extremist content that is driving extremist ideologies, including hate and really hard extremist hatred," she said.

"Everyone is going on about free speech, (but) there is also a risk of extremist ideological content, including those directed at people like the Jewish community and other members of our community."

Ms Spender previously opposed misinformation reforms, saying she thought it was "a very important and delicate line to walk".

She said she would prefer an opt-in method, where users would have to choose the algorithm, rather than an opt-out solution.

Speaking later, independent MP Dai Le said it was up to individuals to assess information, but urged for an option to opt in or opt out of the algorithm.

Opposition frontbencher Tim Wilson says Labor is 'actively seeking to censor' Australians online. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

'Seeking to censor'

However, the Coalition said the clampdown on algorithms would hurt free speech, with opposition frontbencher Tim Wilson on Tuesday decrying it as an attempt to "censor and silence Australians".

"We continue to see attempts to censor Australians by the Albanese government," Mr Wilson said, calling on Labor to put its proposal "on the table".

"Australians need to see it because trust with this government is so low."

It was put to him that members of his own party supported criminalising flag burning, which the likes of former Liberal prime minister John Howard has defended as political expression.

Mr Wilson said it was different.

"The problem we've got is the government is now actively seeking to censor and has been active in censoring, attempting to censor any view they don't like," he said.

Mr Wilson added that the country needed "laws that protect Australia's national identity".

The digital duty of care is also tipped to include mandatory risk assessments and demand companies prioritise child safety in design, threatening hefty fines worth tens of millions for firms that breach their obligations.

"I definitely want Australians to have more choice over their feeds than what they currently have and I want big tech to respect that choice," Ms Wells said on Monday.

"And if they don't respect that choice, I want big tech to suffer big fines."
